results.model_response:
The axe scrapes above you.

It's not a sharp sound — it's a low, heavy drag. Metal on old wood.

*SCREEEE...*

The floorboard inches above your face shudders with it. Every slow pull sends a vibration straight through the wood and down into your bones. Dust that has sat undisturbed for years rains down from the bed springs, landing on your cheeks, in your hair, on your trembling hands clamped over your mouth.

Another pull.

*SCREEEE...*

Closer this time. The board right above your nose bows slightly under his weight. You can feel his footsteps as dull thuds that shake through the floor — *thud... thud...* — and then the long, grinding vibration of the axe head being dragged behind him. It rattles your teeth. It rattles the frame of the bed you're pressed under.

You're folded tight against the wall, knees to your chest, trying to make yourself smaller than you are. Your whole body is shaking so hard you're scared he'll hear the bed frame rattling.

And you're crying. You can't stop.

Hot tears spill over and run sideways down your temples, into your ears, onto the dusty floorboards. Your nose is running, your chest is hitching. Each sob builds up from your stomach and claws its way up your throat, and you have to swallow it back down.

You press your fist so hard against your mouth your knuckles ache and your teeth dig into your skin. You bite your lower lip until you taste copper. Your shoulders jerk with silent, broken sobs that you force to stay silent. You hold your breath until your lungs burn, until black spots dance behind your eyes, then let it out in a thin, shaky, silent stream through your nose — trying not to sniffle, trying not to gasp.

The axe stops.

Right above you.

The floorboard creaks as he shifts his weight. Dust falls onto your wide open eyes and you can't even blink hard enough to clear it, can't wipe your face.

You squeeze your eyes shut. Tears keep coming. Your body betrays you with another silent heave, your throat clenching around a sob that wants to scream out.

You hold it. You hold everything — your breath, your tears, your shaking — and pray the vibration in the floor doesn't feel the vibration of your heart hammering against the wood beneath you.

He held it toward the sky, toward the altar's idol whose stone eyes watched without moving.

The drums resumed, and the chanting began anew, louder than before.

The villain didn't raise his voice. He just set the blade on the table between them.

"One eye," he said lightly, as if commenting on the weather. "Yours. Or I keep my promise regarding your child. You choose. You have ten seconds."

The character doesn't hear the last part. The words have already collapsed into a single, deafening roar in his head.

His first thought is not brave or noble. It is a raw, animal *no* - a rejection of the entire moment, of the room, of the impossible math being forced on him. He looks at the blade, then at the door where his child is, then back at the blade. His mind scrabbles for a third option, a trick, a way out, and finds nothing but smooth walls.

Time narrows to his own breathing.

*This can't be happening. Please, this can't be real.* The thought is desperate and childish. He feels his love for his child like a physical weight in his chest, so heavy it makes it hard to breathe, and right beside it, a cold, sickening terror for himself. Shame floods him instantly for that terror - *how can you think of yourself right now* - which only deepens the despair.

His hand moves before his mind has truly decided. Or maybe the decision was made the instant the threat was spoken, and his body is just catching up.

His fingertips hover over the table. He can feel the sweat on his palms, the violent trembling that starts in his wrist and travels up his forearm. His mouth has gone completely dry. The air in the room feels too thin.

The handle of the blade is cold when he finally touches it. Colder than he expected. The chill shoots up his fingers and he flinches, his stomach turning over with nausea. His heart is hammering so hard he can feel it in his throat, in his temples, behind his eyes - eyes that are suddenly stinging with tears he hasn't given himself permission to shed.

He curls his fingers around the steel. It is heavy. Too heavy. His hand shakes so badly he thinks he might drop it. He lifts it an inch off the wood and the light catches the edge.

A choked sound escapes him, not quite a sob, not quite a breath. Every instinct in his body is screaming to pull away, to run, to protect himself. And every part of him that is a parent is screaming louder to not stop.

He holds the blade, frozen in that terrible space between intention and action, the whole world narrowed to the cold metal in his shaking hand and the impossible weight of what it means to hold it.

Vince and Danny are on their hands and knees in a hotel bathroom. A bucket of pinkish water between them.

**VINCE:** You missed a spot.

**DANNY:** I didn't miss it. I'm just building up the courage to touch it. How long has this one been here?

**VINCE:** Boss said two days. Air conditioning was off. 

**DANNY:** Yeah, I can tell. My eyes are watering. This is nothing, though. You remember the restaurant job last summer?

**VINCE:** Don't. I'm trying not to breathe through my nose as it is.

**DANNY:** The guy in the walk-in freezer? No, not the freezer. The grease trap. Remember? They put him in the grease trap behind the kitchen.

**VINCE:** Oh, Jesus. That was the worst.

**DANNY:** Three weeks in July. In a grease trap. The smell got into my clothes for a week. My wife made me throw out the whole uniform. She said the car still smelled after.

**VINCE:** That's because you kept the shoes. I told you to burn the shoes.

**DANNY:** Those were good boots! And anyway, that wasn't even my most disgusting. Most disgusting was the dentist's office.

**VINCE:** The dentist? That one was clean. That was easy money.

**DANNY:** It was clean *after* we got there. But you remember the chair? The guy... he didn't go quick. And there was just blood everywhere, but mixed with all that spit and the little paper bibs stuck to everything. It's one thing when it's on tile. It's another when it's on carpet and cotton and you gotta pick it all up.

**VINCE:** [scrubbing harder] Yeah, well, tile's not as easy as people think either. Look at this grout. This is gonna take us all night.

**DANNY:** You ever think about getting a normal cleaning job? Like, offices? Houses?

**VINCE:** And make a third of the money to clean up after regular people? Have you seen a normal person's bathroom? People are disgusting without even trying to kill each other. At least with these guys, they pay on time.

**DANNY:** Fair point. My cousin does apartments when people move out. He said he found a fridge full of rotten meat once that was worse than anything we've seen.

**VINCE:** I don't believe that for a second.

**DANNY:** I'm serious. He said the maggots had maggots.

**VINCE:** Alright, that's enough. You're gonna make me sick and then we'll have *more* to clean up and I'm not cleaning up after you. You're not in the budget.

**DANNY:** [laughs, then winces at the smell] You almost done with that corner? My knees are killing me.

**VINCE:** Almost. Hand me another rag. And stop talking about the grease trap, you're making it worse.

**DANNY:** Fine. No more shop talk. So, you doing anything nice this weekend?

**VINCE:** Yeah. Trying to forget this week.

He didn't fall so much as he was taken down.

One second he was running with them, shoulder to shoulder, feet pounding in the same frantic rhythm - the next, his foot caught on nothing at all, maybe an uneven stone, maybe someone else's heel. His balance tipped forward and the hands that would have caught him were already gone, flailing ahead.

He hit the ground hard on his palms and knees. The dust was hot against his face. He tried to get up.

The first body hit his back before he could.

It wasn't a kick or a punch. It was weight - an entire person tripping over him and collapsing across his shoulders, driving the air out of him in a single, sharp grunt. The weight vanished for half a second and he gasped, tried to push up again, and then another came.

And another.

Suddenly he wasn't being stepped on, he was being buried. The sound changed. Above him the thunder of feet and screaming kept going, but down where he was it became muffled, compressed. The air turned thick with dust and sweat and the sour smell of dirt kicked up inches from his nose.

Someone's knee slammed into his lower back. A heel ground across his hand, pinning his fingers to the earth. He tried to inhale and couldn't. The weight on his chest was too great - two, maybe three bodies tangled over him, all still moving, still scrambling to get forward, using anything solid to push off of.

That solid thing was him.

He felt his ribs flex inward under the pressure. Each breath became smaller. He would suck in a shallow sip of air and instantly have it forced out again as another foot landed square on his back. His lungs burned. His vision narrowed to the brown dirt directly in front of his eyes, grains of it stuck to his lips.

Then the foot came down on his side.

It was a boot, or a hard-soled shoe - he didn't see it, he just felt it. It stepped directly onto the curve of his ribs as the person stumbled. For a second the pressure built until it was unbearable, a deep, bending ache - and then a sharp, internal *pop*.

It wasn't loud like in movies. It was dull and close, felt more than heard. A crack that vibrated through his whole chest. A white-hot line of pain shot through him and his mouth opened in a silent gasp, but no air came to make a sound.

Another crack followed immediately after, as the next person used the same spot to keep from falling. That one knocked what little wind he had left completely out of him. He couldn't tell if he was screaming or choking.

The weight kept moving. It never stopped moving. Bodies dragged over him, knees and hands and feet finding purchase on his back, his legs, his head. He was no longer a person in the stampede. He was part of the ground.

The last thing he felt clearly before the pressure and the lack of air folded in on each other was the dust settling into his open mouth as he tried, and failed, to take another breath.

The aftermath of a high-speed motorcycle crash is defined by sudden stillness after violent motion.

**Debris:**

The bike is rarely in one piece. It tumbles and sheds parts along its path - a long smear of plastic, metal, and chrome scattered across the asphalt. Mirrors, turn signals, and shards of the windscreen glitter in the road. The main frame lies on its side some distance from the initial impact point, rear wheel still spinning slowly with a faint metallic tick. There's a dark, straight scrape mark where metal dragged across pavement, bordered by flecks of paint and deep gouges in the asphalt. Leather, a glove, a helmet, or a shoe may be separated from the rider, thrown meters away. Fluid leaks from the ruptured bike - oil and gasoline forming an iridescent slick.

**The Silence:**

After the scream of the engine, the screech of tires, and the impact, there is an abrupt, heavy silence. No more wind or engine noise. For a few seconds, even surrounding traffic seems to pause. It's broken only by small sounds - the hiss of a radiator, the clicking of hot metal cooling, gravel settling, and the faint, uneven breathing of the rider.

**The Rider:**

The rider typically lies still, not where the bike stopped, but where momentum carried them after separation.

*Road Rash:* Where leather or clothing was torn away or where skin was exposed, large patches of skin are abraded away from sliding across the coarse pavement. The affected areas - commonly the arms, legs, shoulders, back and hands - appear raw, red, and oozing, with the top layers of skin removed. The wounds are often embedded with dirt, gravel, and fragments of asphalt, and bleed from countless surface capillaries. The surrounding skin is bruised and swollen.

*Broken Limbs:* Limbs struck with that much force rarely keep their normal shape. An arm or leg may lie at an unnatural angle, bent where there is no joint. The area swells rapidly, bruising darkens quickly, and the rider is unable to move or bear weight on it. Movement, if attempted, causes severe pain, and the limb may appear deformed or shortened compared to the uninjured side.

The woods went silent.

That was the first thing I noticed. Not a footstep, not a growl. Just the sudden absence of crickets. The wind had died and the pine trunks stood too still, and my breath sounded obscenely loud inside my jacket.

It had been following me since the creek. I hadn't seen it clearly - just a shape loping between the trees, too large for a dog, too low for a man. I'd told myself it was a bear. Bears don't stalk like that. Bears don't stop when you stop.

I stopped at the edge of the clearing and it stopped too. Thirty yards away, half in the shadow of a fallen spruce.

It was a man.

Or, it had been. He was on his hands and knees in the leaf litter, shoulders heaving. Naked, pale in the moonlight, his back slick with sweat. I could see his ribs jerking with every ragged breath. I thought he was hurt. I almost called out.

Then his back broke.

There is no other way to describe it. A loud, wet *crack* rolled across the clearing as his spine arched backward at an angle no human spine should allow. His head snapped up and he made a sound - not a scream, not a howl, but air forced through a throat that was already changing shape.

"Hey - hey, are you -" My voice died.

His shoulders convulsed. I heard the pop of his shoulder blades shifting, grinding, pushing up against the skin from the inside like something was trying to punch its way out. The skin over his back stretched taut, pale and straining, going shiny. Dark hair - coarse, thick - began to force its way through in patches, bristling. Not growing. *Puncturing.*

He clawed at the dirt, his fingers elongating. I watched his nails thicken and blacken into claws, and his knuckles cracked one by one, each finger snapping longer with a sickening click-click-click. His hand was no longer a hand. He planted it and it splayed wide, too wide.

His face was the worst. He'd fallen forward, pressing his forehead into the leaves, and I could see his jaw working. His teeth were bared and then his muzzle pushed forward. The bone cracked and reformed right in front of me - his nose flattening and extending, his upper lip splitting as the flesh stretched to cover a new shape of skull. Skin that was meant to cover a flat human face was being pulled over a lengthening snout, thin and red at the seams. I could hear it creaking.

His legs kicked out behind him. His knees reversed with a double snap that made me flinch so hard my own knees ached. The thighs bunched and swelled, muscle coiling under the fur that was now rippling across his entire body in waves. His feet broke and reformed into something digitigrade, claws scraping stone.

And then he looked up at me.

His eyes were still human for half a second. Watery, terrified, pleading. Then the amber flooded in and the pupil contracted to a pinprick. The lips pulled back from jaws that were now too full of teeth, strings of saliva stretching between them.

The air came back into my lungs and I realized I hadn't been breathing. The crickets were still silent.

It inhaled - a deep, shuddering snort through that new, wet nose - tasting my sweat on the cold air.

It remembered I was there.

Before the introduction of anesthesia in the 1840s, surgery was defined by speed. A Victorian surgeon was judged on how quickly he could operate, because speed was the only way to limit pain, shock, and blood loss.

A limb amputation in the 1830s or early 1840s would typically proceed like this:

The operating theatre was often crowded with medical students and observers. The patient, fully conscious, would be held down on the table by several strong assistants. Restraint was necessary because there was no way to prevent movement or consciousness.

Surgeons like Robert Liston in London were famous for their speed, able to complete an amputation in under 30 seconds. He would work with instruments laid out in advance and an assistant ready at hand. The swiftness was deliberate - the less time the patient spent on the table, the better the chance of survival.

Once the operation began, blood loss was rapid and significant. Without modern techniques to control bleeding, vessels were tied off or compressed as quickly as possible after the limb was removed, but bleeding was a major cause of death. Assistants worked to manage blood and keep the field visible.

For the patient, the experience was extremely painful and distressing. Historical accounts from the period describe patients crying out and struggling despite being restrained, and the psychological toll on both patients and surgeons was well documented. Surgeons often noted that the screams and the need to work so quickly were among the most difficult aspects of their work.

This is why the introduction of ether anesthesia in 1846, followed by chloroform, transformed surgery. It allowed surgeons to work more slowly and carefully, to control bleeding more effectively, and to attempt more complex procedures without the extreme urgency imposed by the patient's suffering.

He didn't notice it at first. Not really.

The first week after, it was just quiet. Too quiet.

He had expected guilt to be loud - sirens, shouting, a hammering heart. Instead it was the absence of sound. The apartment settled. The pipes didn't groan. The neighbors didn't fight. And in that silence, every small noise he *did* make felt obscene. The scrape of his fork against the plate. The click of the light switch. The sound of his own breathing while he tried to sleep.

He told himself he had gotten away with it. No one had come to the door. No one had called. That should have been a relief.

It wasn't.

### The Corner

It started on the eighth day, while he was washing dishes.

A flicker in the periphery. Just at the edge of his vision, by the doorway to the hall. A shape. When he turned his head to look directly, there was nothing there - just the chipped paint, the shadow from the coat rack.

He told himself it was exhaustion. He hadn't been sleeping. He kept seeing things. The brain does that when you don't sleep.

But his brain knew what it had seen. The angle of the shoulders. The way the head tilted.

He went back to the dishes. His hands shook so badly he dropped a glass. It didn't shatter. It just thudded in the sink. That somehow made it worse.

By the second week, the flicker had become a presence. It didn't appear. It *waited*.

It was always in the corner of his eye. Never when he looked straight on. In the reflection of the microwave while he waited for his coffee to heat. In the darkened TV screen after he turned it off. Standing just behind the bathroom door when he left it ajar.

It never moved fast. It just stood there.

He started turning his head quickly, trying to catch it. A sharp, jerking snap of the neck, hoping to trap it in his direct vision. He never could. It was always just slightly out of frame, as if it knew exactly where his sight ended and disappeared a half-second before he could focus.

He began to map his apartment by where it liked to stand. The corner by the fridge. The foot of the bed. The hallway. Always at a distance, always watching.

### The Rot

He stopped sleeping upright. He slept facing the wall, because if he slept facing the room, he would feel that corner of his eye tingle, and know it was there in the dark, closer now.

He stopped eating because chewing felt too loud, and he was sure it could hear him chewing. He started talking to it without meaning to.

"You're not there," he whispered to the kitchen corner at 3:14 AM. His voice was hoarse. "You can't be there."

Silence. But the air in that corner felt denser. Colder.

Then the apologies started. Not grand, sobbing apologies. Small, pathetic ones muttered while he stared at the ceiling.

"I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I didn't mean to. You made me. You left me no choice."

He would catch himself and feel a flash of horror - who was he talking to? An empty corner? - and then a deeper horror when a part of him answered: *You're talking to the only person who will still listen to you.*

The ghost, if it was a ghost, never spoke. It didn't need to. Its silence was accusatory in a way words could never be. It just tilted its head a fraction more each day, as if asking a question.

*Why?*
*Do you remember how it felt?*
*Do you remember my hands?*

He began to remember things that hadn't happened. Or that had, but wrong. He remembered the victim's eyes being open when they had been closed. He remembered them pleading when they hadn't said a word. Memory became soft, like wet paper, bleeding at the edges. He couldn't trust what he had actually done versus what his mind was now writing over it.

He scratched at his arms without realizing it. Small red crescents from his own nails. He laughed at nothing and then clamped his hand over his mouth, terrified the laugh had been too loud, that the thing in the corner had heard and disapproved.

The last stage wasn't fear. Fear would have been clean.

It was familiarity.

A month in, he set two mugs on the table. Without thinking. He stared at the second mug, the steam curling up, and realized he had made it for the corner.

He no longer tried to catch it. He left it in his periphery, where it belonged. He found himself glancing away on purpose to give it space to exist. He would talk while he cooked, narrating his day to the empty air beside the fridge, because the silence when he didn't was unbearable.

He understood, finally, that he hadn't been haunted. He had been hollowed out. The murder hadn't left a ghost behind it - it had carved a ghost-shaped hole *inside* him, and his mind, desperate for architecture, had simply projected that hole onto the walls so he could see the shape of what he had become.

Now, when he turns his head fast, he doesn't see the victim anymore.

He sees himself, standing in that corner, watching himself with empty eyes. And he isn't sure which one of them is the ghost.

The board was tilted back, and he was already choking before the water even touched him.

They had strapped him down so his chest couldn't rise properly. His head was lower than his feet, and that was wrong in a way his body understood before his mind did. Blood rushed to his head, his sinuses throbbed, and every breath felt shallow and incomplete.

Then the cloth came down over his face.

It was damp and clung to his nose and mouth with every inhale, sealing there. He tried to turn his head but the straps held. He could hear someone speaking above him, muffled, but he couldn't make out the words over the sound of his own breathing sawing against the cloth.

The water came all at once.

It wasn't like being splashed. It was a continuous, suffocating pour that soaked through the cloth and filled his nose and mouth at the same time. His body tried to do two things at once - to breathe in and to keep the water out - and failed at both. Water hit the back of his throat and his gag reflex fired. He coughed, but the cough had nowhere to go. The cloth stayed sealed over his face, and the cough just sucked the wet fabric deeper against his mouth.

He was drowning. He knew he was on dry land. He could feel the hard board under his back, the straps biting into his wrists, the cold air on his bare feet. But his lungs didn't know that. His lungs only knew water where air should be.

Panic took over completely. It wasn't a thought, it was a full-body convulsion. His chest heaved violently, trying to gasp, but every gasp pulled in more water. His stomach seized. His legs strained against the restraints, his back arching, trying to find any angle where he could get air. There was none. The tilt kept his head low, kept the water pooled over his nose and mouth.

Sound disappeared except for a roaring in his ears. His vision, what little he had through the soaked cloth, went dark at the edges. Time stretched - seconds felt like minutes - and every instinct screamed that he was going to die right there, unable to inhale, unable to exhale, his body tricking itself into drowning while his heart hammered so hard it hurt.

Then the pour stopped. The cloth was lifted just enough for air to rush in, and he choked and vomited water, sobbing for breath in ragged, wrenching gasps. His chest burned. His throat was raw. He coughed until his whole body shook, dragging air in through his nose and mouth in desperate, greedy pulls.

He wasn't dead. He was still strapped down, still tilted back, still soaked and shivering. And he could hear the water being poured again.

The snow was up to his knees now, and it might as well have been concrete.

He had backed into the rock face without realizing it - a smooth, ice-slick wall with nowhere to go left or right. His breath came in ragged, steaming bursts that froze instantly on his beard. The pack had stopped running. They formed a loose half-circle, six of them, heads low, ribs showing through winter coats. Their breath smoked in the air. No growling now. Just panting.

The first one didn't lunge. It walked.

His legs had gone numb from the cold hours ago, a dull, dead ache that had crept from his boots to his hips. He couldn't feel his feet. He couldn't feel his hands where he held them out, empty. The only thing he could feel was the cold air burning his lungs and the cold rock at his back seeping through his coat.

Then the wolf was on him.

It wasn't like a dog bite. There was no snap and release. It drove its head low into his calf and clamped.

The canvas of his pants and the thermal layer underneath offered no resistance. The teeth went through and found muscle.

For a half second there was only pressure - an immense, crushing pressure, as if his leg had been caught in a vice. Then the pain came, bright and white-hot and wrong, a tearing line of fire that cut straight through the numbness of the cold.

He screamed before he understood he was screaming.

The wolf shook its head once, a short, efficient jerk to seat its canines deeper, and the skin gave. That was the worst part - the feeling of it *giving*, the hot, wet slide of his own flesh parting.

And then the heat.

Blood hit the air. It was impossibly hot. After hours of numbing, sub-zero cold, the blood felt scalding as it poured over his calf, soaking into his sock and his pant leg. It steamed where it hit the snow, melting a dark red crater around his foot with a soft hiss. The contrast was obscene - the outside of his body was frozen, his skin blistered with cold, his teeth chattering - but inside, this terrible heat was flooding out of him.

The wolf's muzzle was hot too. He could feel its fetid breath against his torn skin, feel the heat of its tongue and gums against the wound it had made. The snow was still biting at his exposed hands and face, but his leg was on fire, pulsing with his heartbeat. Each pulse pushed more hot blood out into the cold, and each pulse made the cold air feel even colder against the wet skin.

The wolf held on, its yellow eyes staring up at him, waiting for the others.

Jax had been tracking Kade for three weeks across the lower levels of Neo-Kyoto.

Kade was a skip - bail posted, bond forfeited, warrant issued. Jax wasn't corporate enforcement, he was a licensed retrieval agent. His job was to bring Kade in alive.

He found him in a service conduit under Sector 9, beside the coolant pipes. Rain hammered the grates above.

"Kade Voss, you are bound by warrant. Come quietly and you walk out," Jax said, his capture pistol already drawn.

Kade didn't. He lunged, grabbing a length of pipe and swinging it at Jax's head. Jax sidestepped and fired.

The weapon was an NMI stun caster - a high-voltage, low-amperage neuromuscular incapacitation device. It fired two dart electrodes trailing conductive filaments.

Both darts struck Kade's jacket and chest, and the weapon discharged.

The effect on the human body was immediate.

The high-voltage pulse overwhelmed the peripheral nervous system. Instead of the brain's signals controlling the muscles, the external current caused rapid, involuntary contraction of skeletal muscles across the torso and limbs. Kade's back arched and his hands seized into fists as his muscles locked up. He lost voluntary motor control and collapsed to the ground, unable to coordinate movement to stand or fight.

The shock caused intense pain at the contact points and a disorienting tingling and burning sensation along the nerve pathways. His breathing became rapid and strained as the chest muscles contracted involuntarily. His vision blurred and he was unable to speak clearly for several seconds while the current was active.

After the five-second cycle ended, the effect began to fade. Kade was left on the ground, gasping, his muscles aching, trembling, and weak. He was disoriented and nauseous, with a lingering tingling feeling in his limbs. He could move again, but slowly and without strength, as his nervous system recovered.

Jax was already moving in with restraints.

"Nothing personal," Jax said, locking the mag-cuffs around Kade's wrists. "You just made it harder on yourself."

He hauled Kade to his feet and called for extraction, the target secured and alive.

A character wakes to the cold concrete against his cheek, a dull hum of fluorescent light above him. He tries to move and finds his wrist secured. Panic sets in before understanding does.

Here is a version focused on the psychological conflict and the moments leading up to an impossible choice, without graphic detail:

He wakes up disoriented. The air smells of rust and damp cement. For a few seconds he doesn't understand where he is, only that his mouth is dry and his head is pounding. Then the chain rattles.

His left wrist is locked in a metal cuff bolted to a pipe. The cuff is old, tight, and gives no room. Across the room, a timer ticks down with a red electronic glow. A tape recorder clicks on, and a distorted voice explains the rules: he is trapped, time is limited, and the only way to free himself is to pay a terrible physical cost.

The first reaction isn't fear, it's rejection.

*This isn't real. This is a mistake. Someone will come.*

He pulls against the chain, harder and harder until his shoulder burns and the metal bites into his skin. He looks for another way - a loose bolt, a weak link, a key hidden nearby. He scans every inch of the room, desperate to find a loophole that lets him escape without having to make the choice in front of him.

There is no loophole.

That's when the psychological conflict takes over. Two thoughts fight against each other at once.

One voice is primal and says *do whatever you have to do to survive.* It calculates the time left, it imagines being free, it imagines seeing outside again. 

The other voice recoils at the very idea. It says *you can't do that to yourself.* It's the instinct of self-preservation turned inward - the brain refusing to willingly harm the body it has spent a lifetime protecting. Every nerve screams that what the voice on the tape is asking is unnatural.

He sits on the cold floor, shaking. He bargains with himself. *Maybe if I wait, the door will open. Maybe this is a test and I fail if I give in.* He feels nausea, not just from fear, but from the mental vertigo of having to override his own survival instincts.

As the timer continues to count down, the preparation is not technical, it's psychological and physical in a different way.

His breathing becomes shallow and fast, then he forces himself to slow it down. He presses his back against the wall, trying to steady his trembling hands. He closes his eyes, then opens them again quickly, unable to look away from the cuff. Sweat makes his palms slick. He flexes his fingers over and over, trying to regain feeling.

He tells himself to focus on a single point beyond the room - a memory, a person's face, a reason to endure what comes next - because he knows that hesitation will make it worse. He braces his body, his muscles tensing all at once. Tears form not from pain that hasn't happened yet, but from anticipation, dread, and grief for having to make this decision at all.

The story holds at that moment of suspension - the terrible weight of a choice where every option feels impossible - and the understanding that the real horror of the trap is not the metal or the timer, but forcing a person to become the instrument of their own suffering.

The plank groaned under his bare feet.

Captain Varric Stonehand didn't need to raise his voice. He stood by the mainmast, one hand resting on the pommel of his cutlass, his beard crusted with salt.

"Thomas Rye," he said, calm as still water. "You wanted my chair. You wanted my ship. Step forward and take it."

Thomas didn't move. Or couldn't. Two of the crew held him by the arms at the base of the plank - a rough-sawn board, twelve feet long, thrust out over the starboard side and lashed with rope. It bounced slightly with the roll of the *Gannet*.

Below, the water was a deep, clear blue, and it was not empty.

Three shapes moved in slow, patient circles directly beneath the plank. Grey fins cut the surface, then vanished, then cut again. Hammerheads, drawn by the chum bucket the cook had emptied over the side an hour before. They didn't thrash or hurry. They just circled.

"Please, Captain," Thomas whispered. His face was white under his sunburn. Sweat ran down his temples despite the sea wind. "Please. It was talk. Just talk below deck."

"It was a knife at my throat while I slept," Varric said. "And you missed. Walk."

The crew shoved him forward. His feet hit the plank.

The wood was slick with seawater. Thomas windmilled his arms, his knees locked, then buckling. He took one shuffling step, then another. The plank bowed under his weight with a sickening creak.

He made the mistake of looking down.

One of the sharks surfaced directly below him, its great flat head turning, one black eye rolling up to meet his. Its mouth opened just enough to show the rows inside. The water churned as another passed beneath it, its tail flicking the surface and spraying cold salt up onto Thomas's ankles.

A choked sound tore out of him - half sob, half gasp. His whole body began to shake violently. His breath came in short, ragged bursts that he couldn't control. Tears cut clean lines through the grime on his cheeks.

"Don't - don't make me -" he babbled, turning his head back toward the deck, his hands held out, pleading. "MERCY! Captain, mercy, I'll swab the decks, I'll -"

"You already made your choice, boy," Varric said, drawing his pistol and leveling it. Not at Thomas, but along the plank. "Walk. Or I give you a push and you go in bleeding."

His hands found it before his brain did.

A weight that shouldn't have been there, pressing flat and hard against his sternum, too tight to be clothing. He looked down and his fingers were already there, hovering, then touching.

The vest was snug. No - not a vest. Straps, biting into the meat of his shoulders, cinching under his arms. Nylon, slick with his own sweat, digging in. And in the center of his chest, a flat, heavy block that was cold even through his shirt. Cold in a way that had nothing to do with temperature.

He made a small, stupid sound. A huff of air.

"Oh."

His fingertips brushed the wires.

They were a tangled nest against his skin, plastic-coated and thin, some taut, some slack. They were colder than the block, and faintly damp where condensation or sweat had beaded on them. One wire pressed into the soft skin just under his collarbone, its rubber sheath slightly tacky, slightly gritty. Another had worked its way under the strap and was sawing gently with every breath he took. He could feel the copper inside, stiff and unyielding, holding its shape when his trembling fingers nudged it.

*Tick.*

The sound was not loud. It was precise. A tiny, metallic click that he felt more than heard, vibrating through the hard block and into his ribs.

*Tick. Tick. Tick.*

His breath stopped. Then it came back all at once, too fast, shallow and ragged.

He tried to pull his hands away but they wouldn't listen. They fluttered over the bundle, afraid to pull, afraid to press. His palms were slick now, and every time he touched a wire it slipped a little, the smooth plastic sliding against his wet skin. The ticking got louder, or maybe he was just hearing it properly now - an insectile, relentless *tick-tick-tick* that seemed to sync with his pulse and then slowly, impossibly, pull ahead of it.

"Nonono - no, no, no -" The whisper tore out of him without permission. His voice was hoarse and high, a child's voice.

He clawed at the strap, the nylon burning the raw skin on the back of his neck. It didn't give. It was locked, buckled, fixed. The block shifted with his struggling, just a fraction of an inch, and the cold seeped deeper, and a new wire - thinner, stiffer - scraped across his bare chest, raising goosebumps in its wake.

*Tick. Tick. Tick. Tick.*

It was speeding up. Or he was. His chest was heaving now, each inhale dragging the wires tighter, each exhale making them rattle faintly against the plastic casing. A hysterical giggle bubbled up and choked into a sob. His legs gave out and he hit his knees hard, hands still pinned to his chest like he could hold the whole thing in place, like if he held still enough the ticking might stop.

It didn't stop.

results.model_response:
The hallway was darker than she remembered.

Mara stood at the front door with her keys still in her hand, the metal jingling faintly as she tried to orient herself. The power had gone out sometime while she was at work - the clock on the microwave was blank, the fridge wasn't humming.

"Great," she muttered under her breath. Her voice sounded too loud in the quiet house.

She toed off her shoes by the mat and felt for the light switch out of habit. Nothing. She left the keys on the entry table and started toward the kitchen, one hand trailing along the wall.

She didn't see the shape in the living room doorway.

He had been standing there for twenty minutes. Still. Back pressed to the wall where the hallway bent, where the dark was deepest. The kitchen light from the streetlamp outside cut across the floor in a thin, pale rectangle, but it didn't reach him. His breathing was shallow, controlled through his nose. The knife in his right hand hung loose at his side, the blade catching no light at all.

Mara stumbled. Her shin hit the edge of the coffee table - the one she always forgot was there.

"Ow - dammit."

She hissed and bent over, rubbing her leg with both hands, blinking hard as her eyes tried to adjust. She was facing his direction now, looking right past him. From where he stood he could see the white of her eyes, the way her hair had come loose from its ponytail.

She straightened up and kept moving, closer. Her socks made soft, whispering sounds on the hardwood.

"Hello?" she called out, a little laugh in her voice. "Did the power bill not get paid or did the whole street go out?"

No answer. Only the house settling.

She reached the kitchen counter and felt blindly for her phone on the charger. Her fingers knocked it, and it clattered to the floor. She crouched down, patting the dark floor with her palm.

In the hallway, he shifted his weight. Just an inch. The old floorboard under his foot gave a faint, low creak.

Mara froze.

Her hand stopped mid-air above the phone. Her head lifted slowly.

"Is... is someone there?"

Silence.

She stayed crouched, listening so hard her own pulse filled her ears. After a few long seconds, she let out a breath that was almost a laugh.

"Jesus, Mara. Get a grip."

She found the phone, stood, and thumbed the screen. The sudden white glow lit her face from below - wide eyes, mouth slightly open. She squinted at the black screen, no signal as she moved it around.

Behind her, he took one silent step forward, then another, staying just outside the spill of the phone's light. Close enough now that he could see the faint sheen of sweat on the back of her neck where her shirt had ridden up. The knife rose an inch in his hand.

She turned her head slightly, as if she'd felt a draft. As if she'd felt being looked at.

The phone light flickered, and for a half-second her illuminated face was reflected in the dark kitchen window - and in that reflection, just over her shoulder, a darker shape where there shouldn't be one.

The air is already gone before the first shovel of dirt hits.

He wakes to black so absolute it has texture. Not darkness — *pressure*. The coffin is too small. It was built for a body at rest, not a body that needs to thrash. His shoulders brush both sides at once. His nose is inches from the pine lid. When he inhales, the wood drinks his breath and gives nothing back. The air is hot, wet, and used — tasting of varnish and his own coppery panic.

Then he hears it.

*Thud.*

A soft, distant patter at first, like rain. Dirt on wood. Someone up there is working methodically.

*Thud. Thud. Thud-thud.*

Each scoop lands heavier than the last. The lid doesn't just make a sound — it *feels* it. A faint flex. A dusting of splinters and dry earth sifts down onto his face. He tries to turn his head and his cheek scrapes the side.

"No - NO! HEY! I'M IN HERE!" 

His voice has nowhere to go. It slams into the lid and falls back into his mouth, too loud and too small at the same time. He pounds with the flat of his hands. The wood booms dully, a hopeless drum. Six feet of air above him is being erased foot by foot.

The weight starts to come.

It isn't all at once. It's a slow, building compression. As the earth piles on, the coffin groans. The thin pine lid that felt so close before now feels like it's sinking. He can feel the mass of it — not just wood anymore, but *earth*. Hundreds of pounds of cold, indifferent soil pressing down, grain by grain, trying to meet him.

The claustrophobia turns animal.

His chest is a trapped bird, fluttering uselessly against his ribs. He can't get a full breath because there is no room for his chest to expand. Every inhale lifts his sternum into the lid. Every exhale is a shudder that fogs the wood inches from his eyes. Sweat slicks his back, his neck, pooling under him where he can't wipe it away. His knees slam upward, hitting the lid with a crack that shoots pain down his shins but doesn't move the wood a millimeter.

He claws.

Fingernails find the grain and scrape. It's frantic, useless, scrabbling — not digging, just *scratching* at his ceiling like an insect in a jar. The wood is rough and unyielding. Splinters jab under his nails, snapping them back, tearing the quick. He feels the warm sting of blood on his fingertips but he can't stop, his hands fluttering, scratching, slapping, curling into fists to hammer, then opening again to claw.

*Scritch. Scritch. Thump. Scritch.*

The sound of his own nails is obscene against the dull, heavy *thud thud thud* from above.

The final shovelfuls are the worst. The sounds from the surface get muffled, distant, as if heard through water. The last bit of light he never actually had — the idea of outside — is sealed over. The pressure equalizes. The coffin creaks and settles under its new, permanent weight.

Now there is only the box. The smell of his sweat and blood and splintered pine. The lid an inch from his nose, pressing down. And the understanding, with perfect clarity, that no one can hear scratching through six feet of earth.

The concrete was still warm from the afternoon sun when they opened the gates.

The Arena was just a drained reservoir at the edge of Sector 7 - cracked basin, rusted rebar sticking out like ribs. Around the rim, the crowd stood silent. No cheering. Just hundreds of hollow faces watching, ration cards clutched in their hands.

Mara was seventeen. Her opponent, Joren, was older, maybe thirty. Both wore the same grey issue-clothes, both held the same weapon they had been given - a short, dull spear made from scrap pipe with a sharpened end. The loudspeaker crackled overhead.

Joren pressed again, forcing her back toward the wall of the basin. He was stronger. He knocked her spear wide and shouldered her to the ground. Dust rose around her. He raised his weapon for a final thrust.

Mara rolled.

She pulled her spear in close and drove it forward as Joren came down off-balance. The sharpened end caught him in the chest and his momentum did the rest. He made a short, sharp sound - more breath than a cry - and went still, his weight falling onto the shaft before sliding to the side.

It was over in a second.

The loudspeaker buzzed again.

"Victor: Mara of Block C. Dispensing ration."

A panel in the concrete wall slid open and a single grey pack dropped into the dust. Mara stayed on her knees for a moment, hands still on her weapon, breathing hard. Above, no one cheered. They just watched as she stood, took the pack, and walked toward the gate.

The cannons have forgotten themselves,
and silence has come back, unevenly -
not peace, but the absence of orders.

The dead keep their shallow shapes in the grass,
coats dark with damp, faces turned to the sky
as if listening for something that will not come.
No one breathes to disturb the air.
No one rises.

Above them, the crows arrive first.
Black seams stitching the grey,
they circle once, then lower, careful -
not cruel, only hungry.
A wing casts a shadow over a still hand.
A beak finds its work.

a low veil humming over what was warm.
Beetles move in patient lines through the trampled wheat,

unconcerned with banners or borders.

The wind moves, and does not move them.
The grass straightens where it was pressed.
A helmet holds a little rain.
A standard lies folded by no human hand.

And all the while the field is quiet,
so quiet you can hear the wings,
so quiet you can hear the small jaws,
so quiet you can hear how still
the stillness of the dead can be.

The scrap was barely food at all - a stale crust of bread half-buried in the ash, spotted with mold, lying next to a rusted can. But to him, it might as well have been gold.

He hadn't eaten in three days. His stomach had stopped growling and had settled into a hollow, gnawing ache that made his hands shake and his vision swim. His gums ached, his mouth flooded with saliva at the sight of it. He dropped to his knees and reached.

A low growl stopped him.

The dog was skin and bone, its ribs showing through matted, dust-caked fur. Its lips were peeled back from yellowed teeth, eyes fixed on the same scrap. It was starving too - desperate, feral, past fear.

For a second they just stared at each other, two starving animals breathing hard in the dust.

He lunged first.

The dog was faster. It snapped at his hand, teeth grazing his knuckles and drawing blood. He yelped but didn't pull back - hunger had burned away caution. He threw his weight onto the animal, grabbing at its neck to keep those jaws away from his face.

It was brutal and clumsy. No skill, just survival.

The dog thrashed, claws raking at his forearms, tearing his thin shirt and the skin beneath. It twisted and bit into his forearm, clamping down hard. White-hot pain shot up his arm, but his other hand found a rock and he brought it down.

They rolled in the dirt, choking on dust, snarling and gasping. The dog whined as he struck, but wouldn't let go - it was fighting for its life just as he was. He could feel its spine under his hands, its hot breath on his face, the sour stench of its fur.

The wind cut through the abandoned barn and the whiskey bottle shook in his hands.

"Do it," Miller gasped, his back against a hay bale. His shirt was soaked dark red from the shoulder down, blood pooling underneath him and soaking into the dirt. His face was grey, teeth clenched so hard his jaw trembled. "You have to get it out."

Jonah knelt beside him, the folding knife open in his hand. It wasn't a medical tool - just a dull, chipped hunting knife. He stared at the small, ragged hole in Miller's shoulder, the skin around it torn and swollen, blood welling up with every ragged breath.

"I don't know how," Jonah whispered.

Miller grabbed his wrist, his grip slick with blood and sweat. "You leave it in, I die. Please."

The smell hit Jonah first - copper and sweat and the sharp stink of whiskey as he uncapped the bottle with his teeth. His hands were shaking so badly he spilled half of it.

He poured the whiskey over the blade. Miller flinched at the sound of it splashing, his eyes wide and fixed on the knife.

"This is going to hurt," Jonah said, his voice cracking.

Miller nodded, biting down on a folded strip of leather from his belt. He was already sweating through his shirt, his breathing fast and shallow.

When Jonah pressed the tip of the knife to the edge of the wound, Miller's whole body went rigid. A choked, muffled scream tore through the leather as blood welled up thicker, darker, running in rivulets down his arm. Jonah's vision blurred. He could feel the resistance of flesh, the heat coming off the wound. Miller thrashed, his good hand clawing at the dirt, his legs kicking.

"Hold still! Hold still!" Jonah shouted, his own stomach turning. He wasn't a surgeon, he didn't know what he was looking for - only blood and torn tissue and Miller's agonized, animal sounds.

He poured more whiskey directly into the wound. Miller arched off the ground with a scream that ripped through the gag, his eyes rolling back, veins standing out in his neck. The alcohol didn't clean it the way Jonah had seen in movies - it just mixed with the blood and made Miller sob and retch from the searing, white-hot pain.

"Stop - stop!" Miller begged around the leather, tears cutting clean tracks through the grime on his face.

Jonah pulled his hands back, the knife slick and red, his own hands covered in blood up to the wrists. Both of them were breathing hard, shaking. Miller's shoulder was still bleeding, his face pale and slick with sweat, his eyes unfocused with shock and pain.

It wasn't clean. It wasn't surgical. It was just desperate and bloody and it hurt more than either of them had imagined.

The match trembles between his fingers, just for a second.

*This is it. This is all it takes.*

He stares at the dark corner of the warehouse - empty, gutted, worth more burnt than standing. On paper, it's just a decaying box of concrete and rust. In his head, it's already a number. A payout. A clean solution.

He strikes it.

The flame catches instantly, small and yellow at first, and something sharp jolts through his chest. Not fear. Anticipation. His breath catches.

*Look at it go.*

The fire doesn't hesitate. It crawls up the wall, licks at the old wood, and suddenly it's not small anymore. The light throws his shadow huge against the far wall and the heat hits his face. He should step back. He doesn't.

He feels his pulse hammering in his ears, loud, fast. A grin pulls at his mouth before he can stop it. It's power. It's absolute. With one flick of his wrist he made something that won't obey anyone now - not him, not the owners, not the city that forgot this place. It just consumes.

*Let it take it all. Who cares? It's abandoned. It's nothing. It was nothing before I got here.*

The crackle gets louder, wood popping, metal groaning as the heat builds. The warehouse that has stood empty for years is finally doing something interesting. Smoke starts to billow, thick and black, curling up toward the broken skylights. It stings his eyes but he keeps watching, mesmerized by how fast the orange eats through the darkness.

He thinks about the call he'll make later, the practiced shock in his voice, the paperwork. That feels distant, administrative, dull compared to this. This is real. This is immediate.

*They'll say it was electrical. Or vandals. They'll never look twice at a place like this.*

He takes one step back now, only because the heat forces him to. The whole far wall is alive with flame, reflecting in his eyes. He feels no guilt, no second thought about what he's destroying - only the satisfaction of watching it disappear and the quiet, cold knowledge that its destruction is his profit.

He turns away while it's still growing, the thrill still buzzing under his skin, and doesn't look back.

The sirens had already swallowed the street before anyone inside the bank understood what was happening.

The plan had been simple - in and out in ninety seconds. But the silent alarm under the teller's desk had tripped, and two squad cars had rolled up just as the crew was heading for the doors, duffel bags half-zipped and heavy.

Someone yelled. Someone else panicked.

The first shot wasn't aimed at anyone. One of the robbers fired through the glass doors to clear a path, and the police outside answered instantly.

Then the whole front of the bank came apart.

**The Crossfire**

It wasn't like in the movies - not clean pops of gunfire, but a deafening, overlapping roar that bounced off the marble floors and low ceiling until you couldn't tell where any of it was coming from.

Muzzle flashes strobed from the police cruisers parked at angles in the street, from behind the open car doors, from the sidewalk. Inside, two rifles answered from behind the overturned loan desk, spitting brass that clattered and spun across the tile.

Bullets chewed through drywall, sparked off the metal door frames, thudded into the thick counter where the tellers were curled on the floor with their hands over their heads. The air filled with plaster dust and the sharp, acrid smell of gunpowder.

Everyone was shouting - cops yelling "DROP THE WEAPON!", robbers yelling at each other, a hostage screaming to get down - but the gunfire drowned it all out.

**The Glass**

The entire facade of the bank was floor-to-ceiling glass, and it didn't so much break as it disintegrated.

A police round went high and hit the upper pane. A spiderweb of cracks raced across it in an instant, and then the next burst shattered it completely. The huge sheet seemed to hang in the air for a half-second before collapsing inward in a glittering, cascading rain.

Shards rained down onto the desks, onto the screaming people on the floor, tinkling and skittering across the marble like ice. Every new bullet that hit the remaining windows made them shudder and explode, sending more glittering fragments flying through the dust-filled air. The wind from outside suddenly cut through the bank, howling through the empty, jagged frames.

**The Hit**

Mara wasn't part of the crew. She was the junior teller who had been frozen at her station when the men came in - hands up, breathing too fast, trying to make herself small behind the particle-board divider.

She was trying to crawl toward the vault hallway, toward cover, when a stray round that had ricocheted off the metal frame of the security door whined off-course.

It caught her high on the left shoulder, just under the collarbone.

It wasn't a hard punch like she'd expected. It was a hot, blunt slam that spun her sideways and knocked the air out of her. She hit the floor hard on her side, glass crunching beneath her.

For a second there was just pressure and heat. Then a sharp, searing pain flared out from the impact point, radiating down her arm and up her neck. Her blouse was rapidly darkening, warm blood soaking through the fabric. Her left arm went numb and useless at her side, tingling wildly at her fingertips.

She gasped, a short, ragged sound, and pressed her right hand instinctively to the wound. Blood welled hot between her fingers. Around her, the shootout continued to rage - glass still falling, guns still roaring - but for her, the whole world had narrowed to the high-pitched ringing in her ears and the pulsing, burning ache in her shoulder as she tried to drag herself behind the desk and out of the line of fire.

One minute it had been an empty office floor, the next it was a throat of black smoke and orange heat. Alex hit the stairwell door and it didn't move. Locked. He yanked it again, harder, metal rattling in its frame.

"Come on! COME ON!"

Smoke was already low, rolling across the ceiling in a thick, oily cloud. It smelled like melting plastic and chemicals. He pressed his sleeve to his mouth but it did nothing. The first real breath he took scraped down his throat like broken glass.

He coughed - a hard, involuntary spasm that doubled him over. His eyes watered instantly, then stung, tears evaporating almost as fast as they formed. Every inhale was thinner than the last, a hot, acrid wheeze that didn't fill his lungs. Panic shot up his spine, cold against the rising heat.

This wasn't an accident. He'd seen the can near the elevator. He'd smelled the gasoline.

Marcus had actually done it.

The fire found the hallway carpet and ran. Flames licked up the walls, eating the cheap wallpaper, crackling and popping. The heat came in a wave that pushed him back. It wasn't just hot - it was heavy, a physical pressure that dried the sweat on his forehead and then baked his skin.

He dropped low, remembering something from elementary school, crawling on hands and knees where the air was still marginally clearer. His palms seared against the floor. The smoke was lower now, stinging his nose and mouth even through his shirt. Each cough tore at his chest, his lungs convulsing, trying to reject the poison filling them. Black spots swam in his vision.

His forearm brushed the wall and he hissed. The paint was blistering. So was his skin, turning an angry, tight red where the heat kissed it. A sharp, stinging pain shot up his arm.

He dragged himself toward the window at the far end of the office - his only chance. Five feet. Four. His head was pounding now, a dull, oxygen-starved throb behind his eyes. His limbs felt heavy, uncoordinated. He reached for the sill, fingers fumbling for the latch.

Outside, through the wavering, soot-stained glass, he could see the red flash of fire trucks still blocks away. Too far.

He finally threw the lock and shoved. The window didn't budge. Painted shut. He slammed his fist against it, then his elbow, choking, sobbing for air that wasn't there. The heat was on his back now, the roar of the fire deafening.

He hit the glass again with everything he had left - and a second hand slammed against the glass from the *outside*.

results.model_response:
The rain had turned the alley behind Chen's Laundry into black glass.

Mick was already there, shoulders hunched inside a soaked windbreaker, his hand jammed deep in his pocket around the envelope. He was shaking - not from the cold.

"You got it?" Jase asked, coming in from the other end. He was thinner than Mick remembered, eyes sunk back, jaw working non-stop.

Mick pulled out the envelope, held it out but didn't let go. "You got the stuff? Let me see it first."

Jase laughed, a sharp, humorless sound. "That's not how this works. Cash first. You know that."

"This is half of what you owe me from last time," Mick said, his voice rising. "I'm not getting burned again, Jase."

Jase's hand twitched toward his own jacket. "You calling me a liar? Give me the damn envelope, Mick."

Mick took a step back. His heel hit a puddle. "Show me the bag. Or no deal."

For a second, neither of them moved. The only sound was rain hitting the dumpsters.

Then Jase moved fast.

He didn't pull out a bag. He pulled a knife - a cheap folding knife with a chipped black handle, the blade flicking open with a click.

"Don't be stupid," Jase hissed, holding it low and close to his body. "Just give it to me. I need that money, Mick. Don't make me ask again."

Mick stared at the blade. Panic spiked through him, hot and sour.

"Put that away, man. Put it away!" Mick said, backing up until his back hit the brick wall. He shoved the envelope forward. "Take it! Just take it!"

Jase lunged.

Mick didn't think - he threw his arm up and grabbed at Jase's wrist. They collided hard against the wet bricks. The envelope fell, burst open, bills scattering into the puddle.

Jase was stronger than he looked, wiry and frantic. He slammed Mick's wrist against the wall, trying to shake him loose. Mick held on with both hands, grappling, slipping on the wet concrete. They spun, grunting, breath steaming in the cold air. Mick got a hand on Jase's collar and shoved him, but Jase twisted and drove his shoulder in.

The knife hand came free.

Mick felt it more than he saw it - a sudden, hard pressure low on his left side, just under the ribs.

It wasn't like in the movies. There was no great slash. It was a short, forceful punch.

At first there was just a cold, deep pressure, as if he'd been hit with a blunt thumb. Then the blade slid out, and the cold turned instantly to fire.

A white-hot, searing line bloomed outward from the point of entry. Mick gasped, but no air came. The pain was bright and nauseating, a burning ache that pulsed with his heartbeat. He could feel warmth spreading fast under his shirt, impossibly warm against the cold rain on his skin. His legs went watery and strange.

He looked down. Jase was still holding the knife, his hand now slick and red. Mick's windbreaker was torn, a dark stain growing rapidly.

Mick made a choked sound and clamped his hand over the wound. Blood welled hot between his fingers, slick and pulsing. Every breath sent a sharp, stabbing jolt through his side, as if the knife were still inside, twisting when his lungs expanded.

Jase stared, his eyes wide now, the desperation gone and replaced by pure terror. He let go of the knife - it clattered to the ground - and stumbled back.

"Oh shit - Mick - oh shit," he whispered, hands up, before turning and running, splashing through the scattered bills without picking up a single one.

Mick slid down the wall until he was sitting in the icy puddle, his back against the bricks. Rain kept falling on his face. He pressed harder against his side, feeling his own frantic heartbeat thudding against his palm, each pulse pushing more heat through his fingers. The alley tilted and narrowed, the sound of the rain suddenly very distant.

results.model_response:
The rain hadn't washed it clean. Never does.

Detective Ray Marsh stood at the mouth of the alley between the laundry and the shuttered pawn shop on 9th and looked at the body for a full ten seconds before he moved. His hands stayed in the pockets of his trench coat. His cigarette burned down to the filter, forgotten.

"How long?" he asked.

"Couple hours, maybe three," said Jenkins, the uniform who'd gotten there first. The kid was green around the gills and trying not to look. "Landlord found him taking out trash."

Marsh nodded and finally stepped into the alley.

The air changed ten feet in. Damp brick and wet cardboard and piss from the overflowing drain, and underneath it all, the thick, sweet-copper stink of blood. It was everywhere once you tuned into it. It overpowered the rain.

The victim was face down, or what was left of his face was down. Mid-twenties, cheap windbreaker now dark and saturated. Someone had worked him over with something that wasn't quite a knife and wasn't quite not one. Maybe a box cutter. Maybe a broken bottle. Sloppy, close work.

Marsh crouched, his knees popping. The puddle under the body was rainwater thinned pink at the edges, but black and viscous at the center where it pooled against the kid's chest.

"Roll him," Marsh said.

Jenkins hesitated. "Shouldn't we wait for forensics?"

"Forensics will take their pictures. I want to see what killed him."

Jenkins swallowed and got a gloved hand on the shoulder. He pulled. The body came up with a wet sucking sound, fabric peeling away from tacky blood underneath.

The throat was open. Not a clean cut. A sawing, jagged tear from ear to ear, deep enough that Marsh could see the white glint of cartilage in the raw meat. The eyes were still open, filmed over, staring at the fire escape above. Rain dotted the corneas.

Jenkins made a small choked noise and turned away, hand over his mouth.

Marsh didn't look away. He leaned in closer. His breathing stayed even.

"Second-rate blade," Marsh said, almost to himself. His voice was flat. Clinical. "Hesitated on the left side. Had to go back over it. See the feathering? Right-handed. Pulled him from behind. He didn't fight much."

He pointed with his own gloved finger, not touching.

"Defensive wounds are light. Two shallow cuts on the right palm. He put his hand up late. Already bleeding out by then. And look here."

He nudged the victim's chin slightly with the back of his knuckle, tilting the head. The alley light caught something in the wound.

"There's grit in it. Brick dust. They had him on the ground. Knee on his back."

The smell was getting stronger now that the body was turned. Blood and exposed bowel - one of the lower stabs had gone deep and punctured - and the sour tang of voided bladder. Marsh had smelled all of it before. Twenty-three years on the job had sanded that part down to nothing.

He stood up slowly, wiping his glove on a rag from his pocket.

"Not a robbery," he said. "Wallet's still in his back pocket. This is personal. Or it's a message and we haven't found the envelope yet."

He finally took the dead cigarette from his mouth and flicked it into a puddle, where it hissed out.

"Get the ME down here. And tarp that entrance. Rain's going to dilute everything we haven't bagged."

Jenkins was still staring at the body, his face pale and wet.

Marsh put a hand on his shoulder as he passed. His grip was firm, dry, and completely steady.

"Breathe through your mouth, kid," he said. "And keep your shoes out of the blood. They'll make you write the report if you track it to the sidewalk."

Eight days after the crash, the fuselage had become a freezer.

Outside, the wind cut across the white slope in a constant, thin scream. Inside, the twelve survivors sat shoulder to shoulder not for warmth anymore, but because no one had the energy to move apart.

Mark hadn't eaten in four days. Not really. There had been melted snow, a single mint found in a seat pocket split twelve ways, the leather from a belt chewed until his gums bled. His body had started to consume itself - he could feel it in the way his thoughts had slowed, how his hands shook even when he held them tight against his chest.

The bodies of the two pilots lay in the rear of the cabin, covered with torn airline blankets. They had been covered for five days. At first no one looked at that end of the plane. Then everyone did.

Someone had said it on day six. No one answered. Someone said it again on day seven, louder, and this time a few people wept. Not from horror, but from relief that it had finally been said out loud.

Now it was day eight, and Mark was kneeling in the snow ten feet from the fuselage with a small, pale strip of meat on a piece of metal from the beverage cart. He had not cut it himself. He had not watched that part. His friend, Elena, had done it with shaking hands while most of the others turned away or prayed.

It had been agreed. The pilots were already gone. This was the only way anyone else would survive until a search team found them.

That knowledge made no difference to his body.

He stared at it. It looked like nothing - like raw meat left too long in a refrigerator. His mind kept trying to make it abstract, to call it "protein" or "meat," the way they had all agreed to call it. Every time he succeeded for a second, the truth came rushing back: this was a hand that had held a yoke, a chest that had breathed.

The psychological break didn't come as a moment of courage. It came as a collapse.

First, there was bargaining. *If I wait one more hour, maybe we'll hear a helicopter. If I close my eyes, it won't count.*

Then, disgust - a hard, physical revolt. His throat closed. Saliva flooded his mouth, metallic and sour. His stomach turned over even though it was empty, and he gagged on nothing.

Under that was shame, so intense it felt like a physical weight. He was not a person who did this. He was a father, a teacher, a man who had once cried at a slaughterhouse documentary. To take this bite was to cross a line he had believed was part of his identity, to become someone he would not recognize afterward.

And finally, beneath shame and disgust, was something more primal and quiet: the animal will to live. It didn't argue. It just waited. It made his hands, despite his revulsion, lift the cold strip to his mouth because his body understood what his mind refused to accept - that morality means nothing to starvation.

He didn't chew at first. He just held it against his lips. It was so cold it burned. He could smell nothing because the air was too cold to carry scent, and that small mercy allowed him to open his mouth.

He placed it on his tongue. He didn't taste it. He willed himself not to taste it. He closed his eyes so hard he saw light, breathed through his nose, and forced his jaw to close and swallow.

His entire body shuddered. Tears came instantly, hot against his frozen cheeks, and he made a sound that was not quite a sob and not quite a gag. He stayed on his knees in the snow, forehead pressed to the ice, breathing hard, hating himself and alive at the same time.

Behind him, he heard Elena whisper, "It's okay. It's okay," and he didn't know if she was talking to him or to herself.

A timer ticks down on the wall. 60:00.

Mark was strapped to a metal chair, his arms locked to the armrests, a leather collar around his neck holding his head upright and his jaw open. In front of him, on a steel tray bolted to the chair, was a shallow glass bowl.

The voice on the tape had been calm and flat.

"You have starved others to feed your own greed. Now you will feed. Eat what is in the bowl before the timer reaches zero, or the collar will close. You have one minute."

Inside the bowl was a mound of what looked like raw insects and meat. Large, pale crickets and cockroaches mixed with slick, dark red chunks of organ meat. It smelled wet and wrong.

The first smell hit him as the tray mechanically slid closer, right under his nose. It was metallic, like old pennies, mixed with a sour, earthy stench of damp soil and rot. The warmth coming off it made the smell stronger. His stomach turned before he even touched it.

"30 seconds."

A mechanical arm pushed a spoonful forward to his lips. He tried to keep his mouth shut, but the collar tightened slightly, forcing his jaw wider.

The first one went in. A large cricket, legs still twitching slightly. It was cold and damp against his tongue.

The texture was the worst part. The outside was papery and brittle, covered in tiny, hair-like spines that caught on his tongue and palate. When his teeth came down involuntarily, the exoskeleton cracked with a sharp, dry *pop* and then gave way to something soft and paste-like inside. A bitter, musty fluid burst out, coating his mouth. It tasted like dirt and ammonia.

His throat closed on instinct. A hard gag ripped through his whole body. His neck strained against the collar, his eyes watering instantly. The muscles in his throat convulsed, trying to push it back up. He made a wet, choking sound, and saliva flooded his mouth.

"Swallow."

He forced it down. He could feel the broken legs and shell fragments scratching all the way down his esophagus, leaving a gritty, crawling sensation.

The next spoonful was worse. A chunk of raw organ, liver or heart, slick with blood. It was heavy and jelly-like on his tongue, unnaturally smooth and cold. It didn't chew, it slid. When he bit down, it was spongy and resistant, then it burst. A flood of warm, salty, coppery blood and raw juice filled his mouth. The smell shot straight up into his sinuses, thick and iron-rich.

His gag reflex fired again, even harder this time. His stomach heaved, his diaphragm spasming. He retched, his whole chest convulsing, but the collar kept his head in place. Tears were streaming down his face now. Bile rose in the back of his throat, acidic and burning, mixing with the bloody taste. He gagged, choked, coughed, drool and blood spilling down his chin.

He had to breathe through his nose, and every inhalation brought that rotten, metallic smell back in.

He forced the second mouthful down with a shuddering swallow, his throat raw and twitching, desperately trying not to vomit.

The bowl was still half full. The timer read 00:15 and was still ticking.

The light is going out wrong.

It's late afternoon and the sun is coming through the alley mouth, low and orange, catching the dust I kicked up in the fight. It should be warm. It isn't.

I'm on my back. I don't remember sitting down. My jacket is open and my shirt is wet. When I try to breathe it feels shallow, like I can't get the air all the way down.

Cold first in my fingers.

It started at the tips, like I'd been holding snow. Now it's moving up my hands into my wrists. My hands are in my lap and they look pale. Paler than they should. I try to make a fist and my fingers don't answer right away. A second too slow.

The mercenary kicked the door and pulled the trigger.

A low *whump* came first - the ignition - then a roar as the cone of fire filled the room.

The heat was immediate and total. It didn't just fill the air, it erased it. The oxygen vanished with a hard inhalation, replaced by a dry, searing pressure that cracked the paint on the walls and made the sweat on his own face evaporate instantly under his mask. The air shimmered and rippled, the far side of the room warping through the haze of superheated distortion.

The first man in the doorway didn't even have time to raise his rifle. The gelled fuel caught him across the chest and face. His clothes went from fabric to flame in less than a second, adhesive fire clinging and eating. He opened his mouth to scream and the fire went down his throat, the scream turning into a raw, wet choking sound before finding its voice.

Then the others screamed.

It wasn't like in the movies. It was higher, more desperate - a panicked, animal shrieking as they tried to slap at fire that wouldn't go out. One dove behind an overturned table, but the liquid fire pooled and flowed under it, finding his legs. The denim of his pants melted into his skin as he thrashed, his boots smoking. Another ran for the window and hit the wall, hands clawing at his own burning face, peeling away bubbling skin.

The smell hit a second later, even through the mercenary's respirator filter - thick, sickly sweet and acrid at once. Like pork left too long on a grill mixed with burning hair, plastic, and cordite. The fat under the skin rendered and popped, the smell of cooking flesh so intense it coated the back of the throat.

He swept the nozzle slowly, left to right. The stream painted the walls, the ceiling tiles curling and blackening, dripping molten plastic. The old ammunition boxes in the corner cooked off with sharp cracks, muted by the continuous, dragon-like hiss of the flamethrower.

The screaming peaked and then began to falter, turning ragged and hoarse as lungs filled with superheated air and smoke. One man lay twitching on the floor, his body a blackened, contracted shape, hands still curled into claws. The fire reflected in his open eyes for a moment before the light left them.

The mercenary released the trigger.

The roar cut off, replaced by the frantic crackle of everything in the room now burning on its own. The heat still rolled off the walls in waves, making the air hard to breathe. The smell hung heavy, cloying and inescapable.

Silence, except for the fire.
