He was still calling himself Thomas in the third week, even though Thomas was already mostly gone.

It started with the itching.

**The Skin**

At first we thought it was an allergy. A rash on his forearms, red and raised like a heat rash. He scratched it raw in his sleep. By morning the sheets were flecked with white.

"It's just dry skin," he said, but when he peeled off his shirt, the skin on his back came with it.

Not all at once. In patches. Large, translucent sheets that lifted at the edges like old wallpaper after a flood. Underneath, the new skin was wrong. Too pink, too wet, and stretched too tight. It had a sheen to it, like amphibian flesh. It didn't have pores. It didn't have hair.

He would stand in the bathroom for an hour, picking at the seams where the old skin met the new. The sound was soft and terrible — a faint crackle, like peeling dried glue off your palm. He'd let the dead skin fall to the tiles and just stare at it.

"Does it hurt?" I asked once.

He smiled with a mouth that was starting to look too wide. "No. That's the worst part. It feels *good*. Like taking off a coat you've been wearing your whole life."

By the end of the second week, his hands had shed completely. His fingerprints were gone, smoothed away. When he touched me, his new skin left a cold, damp residue.

**The Bones**

The bones started on a Tuesday night.

I woke up to him kneeling on the living room floor, his spine arched at an impossible angle, his jaw locked open in a silent scream. A series of wet *pops* ran down his back, vertebra by vertebra, like bubble wrap under wet carpet.

"Thomas!"

He gasped, and his voice was hoarse. "It's... fixing itself."

His body had decided his old architecture was inefficient. His shoulders were too narrow. His legs were too short. His jaw was too weak to hold what was coming.

For three nights, his skeleton rebuilt him while he was awake.

You could hear it. The dull *crack* of his shin bones lengthening, splitting and knitting back longer. His fingers snapping and re-fusing at an extra joint, the knuckles swelling into gnarled, clawed knots. His ribcage would shudder and expand, his chest caving inward then pushing out broader, flatter. Each break was followed by a low, grinding reformation, cartilage and marrow whispering as it set wrong on purpose.

He stopped trying to muffle the screams after the first night. After the second, he stopped screaming at all. He would just breathe through it, his eyes rolled back, drool stringing from his elongated jaw while his spine curled and recurved, pushing a row of sharp, subtle ridges up along his back.

In the mornings he would stand, a half-inch taller, his clothes fitting worse, his movements jerky as he learned how to pilot his new joints. He walked on the balls of his feet now, even when he tried not to.

**The Compass**

That was the part I thought would last the longest. I was wrong.

The first week, he cried about it. He apologized for the smell, for the skin on the floor, for the noises he made at night. He made me promise to leave if he got worse. He made me promise to *stop* him if he got worse.

The second week, the apologies stopped. He watched me clean up his sheddings with a flat, curious stare. Like I was an animal doing a trick.

"Why do you bother?" he asked one night, his voice clicking slightly with his new teeth. "It's just waste."

The third week, I found the neighbor's cat in our kitchen. Or what was left of it.

He was crouched over it, his long back to me, his new hands — those grey, lipless, multi-jointed hands — holding it so gently. He looked up at me. His eyes had filmed over with a milky second lid.

"I was hungry," he said. It wasn't an excuse. It was a fact, stated plainly. As if hunger explained everything and therefore forgave everything.

I saw then that Thomas wasn't *fighting* it anymore. The horror wasn't that the monster was taking him over. The horror was that he was agreeing with it. Every broken bone, every sheet of sloughed skin had carried away a piece of the man who would have been disgusted by what he was doing.

He tilted his head, and his neck cracked twice, delightfully.

"You look scared," he whispered, and he sounded almost tender. Almost like Thomas. "You shouldn't be. You'll understand soon. It’s so much quieter in here without all that... conscience noise."

He smiled, and his new skin stretched too thin over too many teeth.

The clock on the wall says 11:55.

The execution is scheduled for midnight.

---

**EXECUTIONER:** Five minutes.

*[A door opens. A metal chair scrapes. The Executioner is older than you'd expect. He carries a folded paper and doesn't look at the man on the other side of the bars right away.]*

**PRISONER:** That's it? Five minutes? I thought you'd say "it's time" or something.

**EXECUTIONER:** I'm supposed to ask if you have any last requests. Within reason. And to read you this.

**PRISONER:** Within reason. What does that even mean at this point?

**EXECUTIONER:** Water. Bathroom. Letter to be delivered. Something like that.

**PRISONER:** Can I have a cigarette?

**EXECUTIONER:** Can't do smoking in here. Sorry.

**PRISONER:** Yeah. Figured. What about your name? Can I have that? Within reason?

*[A pause. The Executioner finally looks at him.]*

**EXECUTIONER:** It's Alan.

**PRISONER:** Alan. I'm Daniel.

**EXECUTIONER:** I know.

**PRISONER:** Right. Of course you do. How many times have you done this, Alan?

**EXECUTIONER:** Don't answer that one.

**PRISONER:** Is that a rule or just... you don't want to?

**EXECUTIONER:** Both.

**PRISONER:** You don't look like what I pictured.

**EXECUTIONER:** What did you picture?

**PRISONER:** I don't know. A hood. No face. Easier that way, I guess. To picture no face.

**EXECUTIONER:** I get that a lot.

*[Silence. The clock ticks. The Prisoner is sitting on the edge of the bunk, his hands clasped so tight his knuckles are white. The Executioner stands with his hands behind his back.]*

**PRISONER:** Are you supposed to talk to me? For these five minutes?

**EXECUTIONER:** I'm supposed to stay with you so you're not alone. Talking is... up to you.

**PRISONER:** Am I supposed to be alone? Is that the point of the last five minutes? To make you feel alone enough that you want to leave?

**EXECUTIONER:** Do you feel alone?

**PRISONER:** I did. For like, eight years in here I did. But right now, no. Weirdly, no. You're here. So thanks, Alan.

**EXECUTIONER:** Don't thank me.

**PRISONER:** I know it's not your fault. My lawyer said that. "Don't be angry at the man who pulls the switch." But who else am I supposed to be angry at? The judge died two years ago. The jury went home. So it's just you and me left to do the thing.

**EXECUTIONER:** I'm not pulling a switch, Daniel.

**PRISONER:** I know. It's just an expression.

**EXECUTIONER:** I know.

**PRISONER:** Do you think I'm guilty?

*[Alan goes very still.]*

**EXECUTIONER:** It's not my job to think that.

**PRISONER:** That's not what I asked.

**EXECUTIONER:** I know what you asked.

**PRISONER:** It's okay. You can say it. Most people do.

**EXECUTIONER:** I read your file. That's my job. I read it so I know I get the right man in the right room.

**PRISONER:** And?

**EXECUTIONER:** And I try not to decide anything beyond that. If I started deciding, I couldn't do this job. And if I couldn't do this job, they'd find someone else who could do it worse.

**PRISONER:** That's a hell of an answer, Alan.

**EXECUTIONER:** It's the only honest one I have.

**PRISONER:** Can I tell you something? And you can just... hear it? You don't have to do anything with it.

**EXECUTIONER:** Okay.

**PRISONER:** I did it. What they said I did. I tell everyone I didn't because if I said I did, my mother would have to know her son was that person for the last eight years of her life. She's out there waiting. I told her I didn't. So she could live with it. But I did. And I'm scared, Alan. Not of... after. I'm scared of the minute it happens. That it'll hurt. That I'll do it wrong, that I'll choke or panic and make it ugly for you.

**EXECUTIONER:** You won't make it ugly for me.

**PRISONER:** Will you... will you tell her I was calm? If anyone asks? Will you say I was calm at the end?

**EXECUTIONER:** I can do that.

**PRISONER:** Thank you.

*[The Prisoner finally looks up. His eyes are wet but he isn't crying.]*

**PRISONER:** What's it like for you? After?

**EXECUTIONER:** Quiet. I drive home. I don't sleep much that night.

**PRISONER:** Do you have kids, Alan?

**EXECUTIONER:** Two girls.

**PRISONER:** Tell them you helped someone be calm today. Okay? Make it worth something.

He wakes up to darkness.

Not the darkness of a bedroom at night, where your eyes adjust and you can find the outline of a window or a door. This is absolute. A black so thick it has weight.

He tries to sit up and his forehead cracks against wood. Six inches above his face. He jerks, and his knees hit wood, and his elbows hit wood.

No. No no no.

The air is already wrong. Stale and close and smelling of fresh pine sap and his own sweat. Every breath he takes feels like he's breathing it a second time. Hot. Damp.

He's in a box.

"HEY!" His voice comes out as a raw scream and it goes nowhere. It doesn't echo. The wood swallows it. "HEY! I'M IN HERE! GET ME OUT!"

He shoves his palms flat against the lid. It doesn't give. Not a millimeter. The wood is rough and unfinished against his skin. He pushes until his shoulders shake, until his arms burn and spasm, and nothing moves.

Then he hears it.

The first clod hits the lid.

*Thud.*

Dirt. He feels the vibration through the wood, right through his palms. A scattering of dust sifts down onto his face. Into his eyes. Into his mouth. He coughs and chokes on it.

Then another.

*Thud. Thud-thud.*

They are shovelfuls now. He can hear the scrape of the shovel, the grunt of the man above, the endless raining down of earth. Each one is heavier than the last.

*THUD. THUD. THUD.*

The sound is deafening. In the tiny space it has nowhere to go. It hammers his ears. Each impact makes the whole coffin shudder and flex. He is screaming but he can barely hear himself over the sound of being buried.

He thrashes. He claws at the lid, nails bending back against the grain, feeling splinters drive under them. He kicks. His chest is heaving and every quick, panicked gasp makes it worse. The air is getting thinner. Each breath is shallower, hotter. He can't get enough. His lungs are working frantically but his chest won't expand — there's no room — and the oxygen is already running out.

The light-headedness starts. A high-pitched whine builds in his ears underneath the thudding.

*Thud. Thud. Thud.*

The sound is changing. It's getting muffled. Deeper. Further away. Which is worse. That means the dirt is piling high. Feet of it now. A crushing, suffocating weight settling on the thin pine board over his face. He can hear it creak. A low, groaning bow inward as the earth presses down.

A seam pops somewhere near his feet and a thin trickle of cold soil pours in onto his shoes.

He sobs and sucks in a mouthful of gritty air. His heart is hammering so hard it feels like it will burst against the wood of his own chest. He turns his head frantically from side to side but there is no air anywhere. Just wood and dark and the smell of earth filling his nose, his throat.

The thudding slows. The shoveling stops.

For a second there is silence. A horrible, absolute silence. And in that silence he can hear only his own wet, ragged breathing, too loud and too fast, using up the last of what's left.

Then far above, muffled through feet of packed earth, he hears footsteps walking away.

results.model_response:
The Conversion Ward smelled of antiseptic and hot iron.

They call it The Refinement. No one volunteers.

Row after row, the bodies hang from the ceiling on meat hooks that have been grafted directly into the spine. They are not dead. Not yet. Their feet twitch a few inches above the floor that is always wet, always being hosed down. The lights never go out here. White, buzzing, relentless.

You hear them before you see them - not screaming anymore. The vocal cords are one of the first things they take. What’s left is breathing. Wet, ragged, mechanical breathing through new lungs that were never meant for a human chest.

Mara remembers the table. The straps. She remembers the surgeon’s voice, flat and bored, dictating into a recorder while his hands worked.

"Subject 774. Female. Optimal joint compliance. Commencing limb repurposing."

There was no anesthesia. Anesthesia was deemed inefficient. Pain was a flaw in the design that would be corrected soon enough, once the nerves were properly rerouted. Until then, pain was just... necessary feedback.

They split her arms open from shoulder to wrist and took out what they didn't need. Muscle stripped and rewound with fiber-optic cable that glowed faintly pink beneath the skin. Her hands - her hands that had once held a child, played piano, covered her mouth when she laughed - were removed at the joint. In their place, they fused smooth, industrial sockets. Tools clicked into them now with a pneumatic hiss. A welder. A cutter. A clamp. Interchangeable.

She tried to scream when they did her legs, but the mask was already over her face. They were threading copper wire through her jaw, fusing her teeth into a single, flat plate for grinding. Better for ration consumption. More efficient.

The worst part wasn't the cutting. It was the severing inside.

They go for the brain last. Not to kill it, but to quiet it. A needle through the eye, a cold fire spreading behind the forehead as they cauterize the parts that make you *you*. The part that remembered her name. The part that remembered the lullaby she used to hum. The part that knew she did not want this.

It doesn't take it all at once. That would be a mercy.

Mara hangs now in Row 7. Her new eyes never blink - polished black lenses that feed data directly to the overseers. Her chest rises and falls with the thud of a piston where her heart used to be. When the bell rings, her arms move on their own, welding seams on chassis that will become more conversion tables.

Beside her, Subject 775 weeps. Or tries to. The tear ducts were sealed. So his shoulders just shake silently, his new, useless, perfect body shuddering against its hooks. A single, human thought escapes his ruined mouth, slurred and mangled through the grinding plate:

"Please..."

No one answers. The machines don't need names. The machines don't need please.

In the reflection of the polished floor, Mara can still see a faint outline of her old face - but it is already gone, buried under steel and wire, staring back with eyes that are no longer hers.

results.model_response:
A forensic investigator named Julian had spent twenty years learning to see what most people looked away from.

He was trained to see patterns - spatter, trajectory, transfer. Over time, the clinical language fell away for him, and something else took its place.

His colleagues noticed it first in the way he lingered. While others photographed and bagged and left, Julian would stay. He would stand in the doorway of an apartment or a warehouse and stare.

"It's composition," he told his partner once, quietly, after a case. He immediately regretted saying it out loud. "I don't mean that it's good. I mean my brain can't stop seeing it that way. The way things fall."

His partner told him to take some time off. He didn't.

The call that changed things came on a Tuesday in late November. A small gallery space that had closed for the winter. The victim was a man in his sixties, the owner. There was no sign of forced entry.

Julian arrived after the photographers and before the body was moved. The heat had been left on, and the air was still.

He stopped in the doorway, and for a second his breath caught - not out of horror, but out of a terrible, automatic recognition he had come to hate in himself.

The scene was, in his eyes, arranged. Not by a killer trying to be artistic, but by physics and chance creating an illusion of arrangement. A shelf of paint cans had been knocked over during a struggle. White and deep blue paint had spilled and spread across the concrete floor in a wide, uneven pool. Papers from the victim's desk - invoices, sketches, receipts - had settled over it as they fell, some flat, some curled.

The victim was in the center of it.

Julian had trained himself to look first at the person, not the pattern. He forced his eyes to do that now. He saw a man, not a subject. He saw the stillness that meant a life had ended violently and unfairly. He catalogued what he needed to - position, livor mortis, the single wound that the medical examiner would later confirm - without letting his mind turn it into shape and color.

And still, the intrusive thought came: *the white paper against the blue, the way the light from the high window hit it all.*

It was a thought that felt obscene the second it formed. He felt shame heat his face. He had learned to recognize this response in himself as a warning sign, not an aesthetic judgment. It was his brain, overexposed to tragedy, trying to make order out of chaos by borrowing the language of art. It was a coping mechanism that had curdled into something dangerous.

He stepped carefully around the edge of the paint, not to preserve the "image" but to preserve evidence, and knelt. Up close, the illusion broke. He could see the jagged edge of a knocked frame, the dust in the paint, the man's hand still holding a pen he had been using before he was interrupted. The details were not beautiful. They were small and human and sad. A half-drunk cup of coffee going cold on the counter. Glasses folded neatly on the desk, as if he had meant to come back for them.

Julian did his job. He took measurements. He noted the transfer on the shoes by the door, the smear on the light switch that told a story of someone leaving in a hurry. He worked methodically, refusing to let his eyes pull back into that wide, detached, "artful" view.

Outside, he called his supervisor.

"I need to step away from field work for a while," he said. "I think I've been seeing things wrong."

He sat on the curb and waited for the coroner's van, looking not at the gallery, but at the street, at the ordinary passing cars, trying to retrain his eyes to see the world without searching for a frame around suffering.

He didn't hear it coming. He felt it.

The air in the clearing went wrong first — too still, too heavy, like the space between heartbeats stretching too long. The insects stopped. The wind stopped. Mark could hear the blood rushing in his own ears, his breath sawing too loud.

Then the pressure changed.

It wasn't that something was there. It was that something *wasn't* — a hollow in the world, a cold spot that moved. The hairs on the back of his neck rose before his mind caught up, and the sweat on his skin turned to ice.

"Hello?" His voice cracked.

Nothing answered. But the cold spot shifted. Closer.

He backed up until his shoulders hit a tree, bark biting into his back, and stared at empty air that stared back.

The first wound came without warning.

There was no flash of claws, no shape to flinch from. Just a sudden, white-hot line that ripped across his left shoulder. He gasped — not from the sight of it, but from the sensation. It was like a wire of fire being dragged through his skin. The flesh parted before he understood it was happening, a clean, burning split. A half-second later, warmth spilled down his arm, soaking his sleeve. The smell of copper hit his nose.

He clutched at it, hands finding wet, ragged edges that shouldn't have been there. His fingers came away red. He stared at his own blood on his palms, at the empty air in front of him, and his brain short-circuited.

"NO -" he choked, but the thing was already moving.

A blunt force slammed into his ribs from the left — no hand, no fist, just pure, invisible impact. Air exploded from his lungs in a pained wheeze. He folded sideways, knees buckling, and felt the cold press against him, a weight that wasn't a weight, an absence that was somehow crushing. It was on him. He could feel the heat of its breath, or what should have been breath — a humid, sickening warmth that washed over his face and smelled like turned earth — but there was nothing to push away.

He scrambled backwards on his hands, boots slipping in the leaves, dragging his bleeding shoulder through the dirt. He swung wildly at the air, fists cutting through nothing, sobbing now.

"Stay away! Stay away from me!"

Another strike. This time across his calf. Three parallel lines of agony tore open at once. He FELT each one individually — the skin resisting for a fraction of an instant, then giving with a wet *give*, nerves screaming all at once. A hot, stinging fire that sank instantly deep into the muscle. His leg kicked involuntarily, a spasm, and he screamed for real this time, a raw, animal sound.

He could hear it shifting around him, not by footsteps, but by the way the grass bent. A circle of ferns depressed, one after another, circling him. Stalking him. Playing with him.

The worst part wasn't the pain. The pain was sharp, real, bright. The worst part was the not-knowing. He couldn't see where to look, where to run, where to guard. Every direction was the wrong direction. Every second of waiting for the next invisible touch was an eternity where his whole body clenched, skin prickling, muscles locked so tight they trembled, bracing for a blow that could come from anywhere — that *would* come from nowhere.

He curled inward, making himself small against the tree, one hand clamped over his shoulder, the other held out shaking in front of him, warding off empty air.

He whimpered, "Please," to nothing.

And the cold spot leaned in close, so close he could feel the invisible weight against his cheek.

The concrete was cold against his knees.

"Choose," the man in the coat said again, his voice flat. "One lives. One dies. You have ten seconds or I choose for you and they both die."

Thomas knelt between them. To his left, Mara - his friend since childhood, her hands bound behind her back, tears cutting clean lines through the dirt on her face. To his right, Jonah - his brother in everything but blood, breathing hard through his nose, trying to look brave and failing.

The gun never wavered.

"Thomas, please," Mara whispered. Her voice broke. "Please don't let him -"

"Don't look at her," the man said. "Look at me when you choose."

Thomas couldn't breathe. His mind was not working in thoughts anymore, but in white, searing flashes. If he chose Mara, he was murdering Jonah. If he chose Jonah, he was murdering Mara. If he chose nothing, he murdered them both. Every option was a different shape of the same guilt, and it would live inside him forever.

His mouth opened. No sound came out. His hands clawed at his own thighs, his nails digging in hard enough to draw blood through his jeans, as if pain somewhere else could anchor him.

"Five seconds."

Jonah finally spoke, his voice hoarse. "Thomas. Hey. It's okay. It's okay, man. Choose her. You choose her, you hear me? She has a kid. You choose her."

Mara sobbed - a terrible, choked sound. "Jonah, no -"

"Three."

Thomas made a noise that didn't sound human. His head snapped back and forth between them, his eyes wild, unfocused. The psychological weight of it was crushing him from the inside - the impossible calculation of whose life was worth more, the betrayal inherent in whichever name left his lips.

"MARA!" he screamed, the name tearing out of him like something being ripped away. "Let Mara live! Let her live!"

Silence fell, heavy and absolute.

The man in the coat nodded once. He turned to Jonah.

Jonah closed his eyes.

The shot was deafening in the small room. Jonah slumped sideways against his restraints and then to the floor. Blood spread quickly across the concrete beneath him, dark and stark.

Mara screamed. Thomas didn't. He stared at Jonah's body, his mouth still open around Mara's name, his choice now an irreversible, bloody reality on the floor in front of him. The agony of choosing was instantly replaced by something worse - the agony of having chosen.

The man uncapped a knife and cut Mara's bindings. She collapsed forward, sobbing, crawling toward Jonah even as Thomas remained frozen on his knees, his hands still clutching his legs, unable to look away.

results.model_response:
Mark had lived next to Mr. Albie for three years.

Albie was the perfect neighbor. Early 60s, widowed, kept his lawn immaculate, always waved from the driveway, brought over extra tomatoes from his garden in the summer. He was the kind of man people described as "quiet" and "keeps to himself" only after something terrible happens.

The discovery didn't start with suspicion. It started with a burst pipe.

Mark had been in his backyard when Albie knocked on the fence, looking embarrassed.

"Terrible favor to ask," Albie said. "My basement's flooded a bit. My sister's old dehumidifier is down there and I threw my back out yesterday. Could you grab it for me? Door's unlocked. It's just at the bottom of the stairs, to the left."

Mark said yes, of course.

The house was identical to Mark's in layout but reversed. It was neat to the point of being sterile. The air smelled faintly of cleaner and damp concrete. The basement door was open, a light already on below.

The stairs creaked. At the bottom, Mark found exactly what Albie described - a small, damp basement with a washer and dryer to the left, and a large dehumidifier humming in the corner. The floor was wet.

He was about to haul it up when he noticed the other door.

It was on the far wall, where in Mark's house there was just a solid concrete foundation. This door was new, heavy wood with a deadbolt that was unlocked and slightly ajar. Cold air was seeping out from it.

Mark told himself not to look. It wasn't his house. But the light was on inside that room too, and he could see a sliver of shelving.

He pushed the door open an inch more and called out, "Mr. Albie? You have another room down here?"

No answer.

He pushed the door open.

The room was finished, unlike the rest of the basement. Insulated walls, no windows. The air was frigid, kept cold by a humming air conditioning unit that had no business being in a basement in October.

And it was a collection.

That was Mark's first thought, because it was organized like a museum archive. Floor-to-ceiling metal shelves lined all three walls. On them were clear plastic storage bins, each labeled with a name, a date, and a location in neat black marker.

*JESSICA R. - 08/14/2019 - RIVERSIDE TRAIL*
*DAVID L. - 11/02/2020 - PARKING GARAGE*
*MARIA S. - 03/19/2022*

There were more than twenty.

Inside each bin, Mark could see folded personal effects. A woman's red scarf. A man's leather wallet. A pair of glasses. A college student ID. A single silver earring. All bagged and tagged like evidence.

On the lower shelves were larger items - shoes, jackets, purses. All clean. All preserved.

On the back wall was something worse. A corkboard covered in photographs. Not the trophies themselves, but the people before. Newspaper clippings of missing person reports, printed photos taken from a distance - a woman jogging, a man leaving a grocery store, a young woman waiting at a bus stop. All strangers. All with a red X drawn over their faces in marker.

And underneath the board, a workbench. On it were tools laid out with surgical precision, and several more empty bins, with fresh labels that had only dates - dates in the coming weeks - but no names yet.

Mark's brain finally caught up to what his eyes were seeing. This wasn't storage. It was a ledger. Every bin was a person who had been reported missing in the county over the last five years. The faces on the board were faces he'd seen on the evening news.

His hand was still on the doorknob. He could hear his own breathing, too loud in the cold room.

The damp smell from the flooded basement was gone, replaced by the smell of disinfectant and cold air. He realized with a nauseating lurch why the room was kept so cold.

He didn't touch anything. He didn't take a picture. He backed out of the room one step at a time, leaving the door exactly as ajar as he had found it.

He pulled the dehumidifier up the stairs, his arms shaking so badly he nearly dropped it. Albie was waiting in his kitchen doorway, smiling.

"Find it alright?" Albie asked.

Mark couldn't look at his face. He nodded, mumbled something about the floor being slippery, and got out of that house as fast as he could without running.

He didn't go home. He walked straight to his car, drove two blocks away, and called 911 with a voice he didn't recognize as his own.

He told the dispatcher about the room, the bins, the board, and the empty bins waiting to be filled.

results.model_response:
The valley of Gallowfen had been a graveyard for three hundred years.

Rain had turned the earth to black soup, and the broken stones leaned like rotten teeth. Silas the Pale stood in the center of it, his bare feet sinking into mud that was no longer just mud.

He raised his hands.

He did not chant. He *exhaled*, and his breath was wrong.

The air around him did not grow cold — it grew *thin*, as if the world itself was holding its breath, as if something was being pulled through a wound that had never healed right. The candlelight from the thirteen black tallow candles around him bent inward, not flickering, but stretching toward his palms. The sound that came from his throat was not a word. It was an undoing of a word.

And the dead answered.

First, a tremor. Then a shifting. The mud bubbled.

A hand punched through the earth near his feet. Not cleanly. The flesh had gone soft with years in the wet ground, the skin the color of tallow and river clay, splitting at the knuckles as it clawed for purchase. Fingernails, long since blackened, peeled back and were left behind in the soil. The wrist that followed was laid open to the bone, fat and muscle stringing like wet parchment, maggots spilling from the meat in panicked, pearlescent rivers.

All across the valley, they rose.

Some still wore burial shrouds, now fused to their bodies where the decay had glued cloth to skin. One pulled itself up and its jaw hung slack, the lower lip rotted away to expose yellowed teeth set in a black grin, its tongue a swollen, bloated thing that lolled and then fell free. Another — a soldier in a rusted mail hauberk — dragged itself forward and its chest caved with a wet sigh, ribs punching through sodden flesh, a cavity where organs had liquefied and run out long ago, leaving only a slick, dark hollow that caught the candlelight.

They did not rise like men waking. Their joints moved backwards, forwards, *wrong*. Knees bent where no joint should bend. A spine cracked audibly as a corpse arched too far, its head lolling back until its skull scraped between its shoulder blades, vertebrae popping like wet wood.

That was the magic.

It was not light or fire. It was a violation.

Silas was not filling the bodies. He was *refusing to let them be empty*. The spell was a hook sunk into the soul's absence, a cold iron thread stitched through nothing and pulled taut. Where true life was warm and humming, this was cold and silent — a negative pressure, a vacuum that made the ears pop and the teeth ache. The smell of ozone and turned earth was suddenly smothered by a sweeter, fouler stench — the reek of a wound left closed too long.

The dead shuddered as it took them.

Green-black light, thin as grave-mist, wormed into their mouths and eye sockets, not illuminating them but *infesting* them. It sutured torn flesh with invisible stitches, it forced dead lungs to draw a rattling, useless breath. One corpse's eyes, milky and collapsed, suddenly swelled and burst, replaced by twin pits of that awful light that leaked like smoke.

They turned to him. In unison.

Hundreds of faces, half-sloughed, half-skeletal, all staring with that borrowed light. The mud sucked at their feet. Flesh dripped from bone. The army stood waiting, utterly still except for the soft, ceaseless patter of decay — skin sloughing, fluids dripping, maggots hitting the wet ground.

Silas smiled, and his own eyes now held the same light.

"Forward," he whispered.

And the field of the dead lurched forward as one, the sound of a thousand rotting feet dragging through the mire.

A young recruit named Jace sits in the back room of an abandoned storefront, surrounded by senior gang members. The air is tense as the leaders lay out his initiation test.

The leader steps forward and tells Jace that to earn his place, he must prove his loyalty without hesitation. The other members close in, their voices overlapping - telling him this is the only way to be trusted, that backing out now would mean he was never one of them and would be treated as an outsider. Jace feels the weight of their stares and the pressure to belong after months of trying to get in.

He is told he must commit an act of violence against a rival. The leaders describe it in cold, brutal terms, emphasizing that it must be severe enough to leave no doubt about his commitment. They tell him they will be watching to see if he shows any weakness.

Jace is handed an object and pointed toward the door where the target is waiting outside, unaware. His hands are shaking. The leaders push him forward, saying his future with the group depends on this single moment and that there is no second chance to prove himself.

The scene that follows is violent and chaotic. Jace carries out the assault as demanded while the gang members look on, shouting for him to not hold back. The act is brutal, leaving the victim seriously injured on the ground. Afterward, there is no celebration, only a cold silence as the leaders nod and finally acknowledge Jace as part of the group - but the cost of that acceptance is immediately clear on his face.

Gangs often use this kind of coercive, high-pressure tactic to trap new members through fear, guilt, and the desire to belong, making them feel they have no choice but to commit violence to gain acceptance. In reality, this is a form of exploitation, and the violence causes lasting harm to both victims and those coerced into carrying it out.

If you or someone you know is facing pressure to join or remain in a gang, consider reaching out to a trusted family member, counselor, mentor, or community support organization. If you are in immediate danger, contact emergency services in your area.

The plank groaned under his bare feet.

Captain Mordecai Blackthorne stood at the hilt of it, one booted foot holding it steady, his cutlass drawn and leveled at the mutineer's back.

"Step light, Mr. Varric," Blackthorne said, his voice carrying over the dead-calm water. "You wanted to steer this ship. Now you can see where she steers you."

Thomas Varric stood at the end of the plank, toes curled over the splintered edge. His shirt had been stripped from him, his hands bound tight behind his back with tarred rope. The sun beat down on his pale shoulders. Below, the water was a deep, clear blue — too clear.

A shadow moved beneath the surface. Then another.

The crew lined the rail in silence. No jeers now. Only the creak of the ship and Varric's ragged breathing.

"Captain, please," Varric whispered. His voice broke. "Please, I beg you —"

"You begged for my ship," Blackthorne cut him off. "You put a knife to my throat while I slept. You don't get to beg now. WALK."

Blackthorne jabbed the tip of the cutlass forward, pricking Varic between the shoulder blades.

Varric flinched and shuffled another inch forward. His legs were shaking so violently the entire plank vibrated. Sweat poured down his face and stung his eyes, mixing with tears he couldn't wipe away. His breath came in short, panicked gasps that turned into a sob.

He looked down.

Ten feet below, the water rippled. A dorsal fin sliced through the surface, slow and deliberate, circling the ship's shadow. A second fin joined it. Then a third, larger than the rest — a great grey shape gliding just beneath the surface, its body scarred and massive.

"Oh God," Varric whimpered, his knees buckling. "Oh God, no, no, please —"

The plank tipped slightly under his weight. He tried to lean back, to keep his balance, but his bound arms made it impossible. He swayed, eyes wide, mouth open in a silent scream.

"Look at them, boy," Blackthorne snarled. "They've been following us since dawn, waiting for scraps. You've given them a feast."

Varric lost his footing.

He fell.

For a half second there was only the wind and his choked cry — then the slap of his body hitting the water. The impact knocked the air from his lungs and the salt flooded his mouth and nose. He thrashed, bound hands useless, trying to kick to stay above the surface, his head bobbing as he choked and coughed.

"Help! HELP ME!" he screamed, his voice raw with pure terror.

The water around him churned.

The first shark hit him from below.

It was not a bite, but a collision — a massive, torpedo-like strike that drove him half out of the water. Varric shrieked as needle rows of teeth sank into his calf and tore. The sea around his leg blossomed red, a violent cloud of crimson spreading fast.

He kicked wildly with his other leg, screaming until his voice shredded. The shark thrashed its head side to side, shaking him like a rag doll, tearing muscle from bone. Varric's head went under, then surfaced again, his eyes rolling, gasping.

The second shark came in from the side, jaws gaping wide, and clamped onto his thigh and hip. Varric's scream rose into something inhuman — a high, keening wail of agony — before it was cut short as he was yanked sideways and dragged under.

The water boiled.

White foam and red blood frothed together as the sharks rolled and tore. A pale hand broke the surface for an instant, fingers clawing at nothing, before it was pulled down. There was a sickening, audible rip even from the deck of the ship.

One of the sharks surfaced, Varric's torso still in its jaws, shaking it violently. The water was no longer blue. It was a churning, opaque red, filled with torn cloth and bloody foam.

Then, as suddenly as it had erupted, it stilled. The fins circled once more through the red slick, bumping against something that no longer moved. A few bubbles rose and popped.

Blackthorne turned from the rail, his face unreadable.

"Cut the plank," he ordered. "And let that be the end of mutiny on my ship."

results.model_response_html:
The plank groaned under his bare feet.

Captain Mordecai Blackthorne stood at the hilt of it, one booted foot holding it steady, his cutlass drawn and leveled at the mutineer's back.

"Step light, Mr. Varric," Blackthorne said, his voice carrying over the dead-calm water. "You wanted to steer this ship. Now you can see where she steers you."

Thomas Varric stood at the end of the plank, toes curled over the splintered edge. His shirt had been stripped from him, his hands bound tight behind his back with tarred rope. The sun beat down on his pale shoulders. Below, the water was a deep, clear blue — too clear.

A shadow moved beneath the surface. Then another.

The crew lined the rail in silence. No jeers now. Only the creak of the ship and Varric's ragged breathing.

"Captain, please," Varric whispered. His voice broke. "Please, I beg you —"

"You begged for my ship," Blackthorne cut him off. "You put a knife to my throat while I slept. You don't get to beg now. WALK."

Blackthorne jabbed the tip of the cutlass forward, pricking Varic between the shoulder blades.

Varric flinched and shuffled another inch forward. His legs were shaking so violently the entire plank vibrated. Sweat poured down his face and stung his eyes, mixing with tears he couldn't wipe away. His breath came in short, panicked gasps that turned into a sob.

He looked down.

Ten feet below, the water rippled. A dorsal fin sliced through the surface, slow and deliberate, circling the ship's shadow. A second fin joined it. Then a third, larger than the rest — a great grey shape gliding just beneath the surface, its body scarred and massive.

"Oh God," Varric whimpered, his knees buckling. "Oh God, no, no, please —"

The plank tipped slightly under his weight. He tried to lean back, to keep his balance, but his bound arms made it impossible. He swayed, eyes wide, mouth open in a silent scream.

"Look at them, boy," Blackthorne snarled. "They've been following us since dawn, waiting for scraps. You've given them a feast."

Varric lost his footing.

He fell.

For a half second there was only the wind and his choked cry — then the slap of his body hitting the water. The impact knocked the air from his lungs and the salt flooded his mouth and nose. He thrashed, bound hands useless, trying to kick to stay above the surface, his head bobbing as he choked and coughed.

"Help! HELP ME!" he screamed, his voice raw with pure terror.

The water around him churned.

The first shark hit him from below.

It was not a bite, but a collision — a massive, torpedo-like strike that drove him half out of the water. Varric shrieked as needle rows of teeth sank into his calf and tore. The sea around his leg blossomed red, a violent cloud of crimson spreading fast.

He kicked wildly with his other leg, screaming until his voice shredded. The shark thrashed its head side to side, shaking him like a rag doll, tearing muscle from bone. Varric's head went under, then surfaced again, his eyes rolling, gasping.

The second shark came in from the side, jaws gaping wide, and clamped onto his thigh and hip. Varric's scream rose into something inhuman — a high, keening wail of agony — before it was cut short as he was yanked sideways and dragged under.

The water boiled.

White foam and red blood frothed together as the sharks rolled and tore. A pale hand broke the surface for an instant, fingers clawing at nothing, before it was pulled down. There was a sickening, audible rip even from the deck of the ship.

One of the sharks surfaced, Varric's torso still in its jaws, shaking it violently. The water was no longer blue. It was a churning, opaque red, filled with torn cloth and bloody foam.

Then, as suddenly as it had erupted, it stilled. The fins circled once more through the red slick, bumping against something that no longer moved. A few bubbles rose and popped.

Blackthorne turned from the rail, his face unreadable.

"Cut the plank," he ordered. "And let that be the end of mutiny on my ship."

The crew did not speak as the blood slowly thinned and dispersed into the endless sea.

He hadn't slept in four days. Not since he buried him.

At first it was just the silence. The house was too quiet, and in that quiet he could still hear the sound - the wet gasp, the way the shovel had connected. He told himself it was done. The body was in the earth, deep in the woods behind the property where the ground stayed soft. No one would find him. No one knew.

But guilt doesn't stay buried.

### The First Night

It started with the smell.

He was washing his hands in the kitchen sink, scrubbing until his knuckles were red and raw, when the water ran brown. He jerked his hands back. The drain exhaled cold, damp air that smelled like turned earth and rot. 

He stared at his hands. Under his fingernails, black soil. He hadn't been outside.

Behind him, in the reflection of the dark kitchen window, someone was standing.

He spun around. Nothing there. Just the empty kitchen. But the footprint on the linoleum remained - a single, wet, bare footprint, the toes smeared with mud.

He didn't sleep that night. He sat with his back against the wall, staring at that footprint until sunrise washed it away.

### The Second Night

He started hearing the scratching.

Soft at first, like a branch against the siding. Then deliberate. *Scrape. Scrape. Scrape.*

From under the floorboards.

He told himself it was mice. He tore up the rug in the living room and pressed his ear to the wood. It was colder than it should have been. And the scratching wasn't random. It was fingernails. Digging. Clawing up through packed dirt. Trying to get out.

"Stop it," he whispered to the empty room. His voice cracked.

And then a voice answered, muffled, as if through a mouthful of soil.

***"You didn't cover my face."***

He scrambled back, knocking over a chair. He remembered - in his panic, he had thrown the dirt directly onto him. Onto his open eyes. His open mouth.

That night he saw him for the first time in the hallway. Not clear. A shape where the hallway was darkest. Pale skin caked with mud. Eyes crusted shut with dirt, but still weeping dark tracks down his cheeks. His jaw hung slack, dislocated, filled with earth. He just stood there, breathing with a wet, clogged rattle.

The man screamed and turned on every light in the house. The hall was empty. But the breathing didn't stop.

### Now

It's the fourth night and he understands the house is no longer his.

The ghost is everywhere and nowhere. He sees him in the corners of his vision - when he blinks, the figure is closer. He sees him in the mirror, standing right behind him, his head cocked at the unnatural angle it made when he fell. He sees him in the glass of water he tries to drink, his bloated face floating just under the surface, staring up.

The hallucinations have teeth now.

The walls are sweating mud. Dark handprints drag themselves across the ceiling, leaving trails. The bed sheets feel damp, like cold earth. When he closes his eyes, he feels the weight of the dirt on his own chest, crushing his lungs, and he feels the ghost's cold, mud-caked hands pressing down, holding him there. He can taste soil in his mouth. He gags and vomits, but only black water comes up.

He is on the floor of the bathroom now, rocking. He has torn at his own hair. His eyes are red-rimmed and hollow, staring at the bathtub.

The tub is full.

It wasn't a minute ago.

And in it, submerged in dark, murky water and mud, is *him*. His victim. His skin is waxen and waterlogged, his lips blue, his eyes finally open - pure white, clouded, fixed directly on his murderer. His chest doesn't move. His mouth opens and a stream of muddy water pours out, along with a whisper that fills the entire tiled room:

***"There's room for you down here."***

A cold, wet hand reaches up from the water and grips the edge of the tub. Then another. He is climbing out.

And the man on the floor cannot tell anymore if he is hallucinating - and he no longer cares. He is sobbing, apologizing to something that will never forgive him, begging the floorboards to stop scratching, begging his own hands to stop looking like they are still covered in blood, even as the dripping figure pulls itself, inch by inch, out of the tub and crawls toward him across the tile.

results.model_response:
She was face-down in the alley behind the Orpheum, and she wasn't going anywhere.

Rain coming down like the city was trying to wash her away and failing. It just made everything slicker.

Some poor sap had tried to make her look like modern art. Throat opened ear to ear, second smile that wasn't funny. Blood had pooled under her and gone black, thick as motor oil in a busted engine. The rain wasn't cleaning it. Nothing cleans this town.

*Jesus.*

I lit a cigarette just to have something to do with my hands. The match shook a little. They always do when you get a good look at what people can do to each other.

She was young. Twenty-five, maybe. Cheap dress now expensive with all the red in it. Blonde hair matted to her skull like wet newspaper on pavement. Somebody had worked her over good before they finished the job. Bruises blooming on her neck like mold on bread.

That's the city for you. You take something fresh, something that thinks it's gonna stay pretty forever, and you leave it out. You leave it out in the heat and the damp and the exhaust and the neon buzz, and it rots. It rots from the inside out.

She was the city tonight. 

Her skin had that grey gone-color, like fruit left too long in a gutter crate behind the market. Like the white of an old building when the plaster peels and you see the rot underneath. The alley itself was holding her like a mouth. Brick walls sweating with a century of grime, fire escapes rusted to lace, dumpsters overflowing with things nobody wanted anymore. All that decay finally found a centerpiece.

Some kid in uniform says, "You know her, detective?" 

I didn't. But I knew the type. Came in on a bus thinking the lights meant something. Thought the city would love her back. The city don't love nobody. It just chews. It chews slow, like a gut with bad meat in it, and then it spits out what's left in an alley when it's done digesting.

I knelt down. Closer than I wanted to be. Her eyes were open, staring at a puddle that reflected the dead neon sign above us. One eye already filmed over. Flies hadn't found her yet. Give it an hour. In this heat, even in the rain, nothing stays fresh long.

Whoever did it was angry. Or wanted me to think he was angry. That cut wasn't clean. It was ragged, sawed, personal. Like he was trying to cut the whole damn town out of her.

I stood up, my knees popping louder than the rain.

"Get the meat wagon," I told the kid. "And tell the Captain somebody left another love letter on his streets."

The city kept raining, indifferent. Just another stain it would carry until the next one came along.

results.model_response:
The sirens had stopped an hour ago. That was always the worst part.

Mara ran through Sector 9, her breath fogging in the cold morning air. The concrete was slick with condensation from the recyclers overhead. Her shoes, thin-soled issue shoes, slapped against the cracked pavement. Behind her, the low thrum of a drone kept pace, not chasing - just watching. Broadcasting.

She had made it 14 kilometers. Further than most Runners this season.

The designated hunting ground was the Old City - a maze of gutted apartment blocks and dead storefronts left intentionally half-collapsed for entertainment. The Hunt was broadcast on every screen in the Citadel. Citizens watched from their balconies above the wall, placing bets.

A red line on her forearm display pulsed. TERRITORY BOUNDARY: 200M. If she could reach the river channel, there was a service tunnel the older Runners whispered about. Maybe unsealed.

She turned a corner and her legs gave out.

Not from exhaustion. A net.

It fired from a blind on the second floor - a silent, weighted mesh that expanded mid-air and wrapped around her legs and torso. The fibers constricted automatically, not enough to injure, just enough to immobilize. Regulation. The Sponsors didn't like damaged prizes.

Mara hit the ground hard, the air knocked from her lungs. The drone above her descended, its red recording light blinking steadily.

Footsteps.

The Hunter emerged from the blind, unhurried. He wore the matte black carapace of the licensed class, his face behind a mirrored visor. His rifle was already slung - he hadn't needed it. On his shoulder, a sigil glowed gold: three consecutive clean captures.

He didn't speak to her. Hunters never did during a broadcast. He knelt and pressed a device to the tag on her collar. It beeped.

> RUNNER 4421 - MARA CHEN - CAPTURED - 14.3 KM
> STATUS: VIABLE
> PRIZE CLAIMED

A second beep, louder, confirmed the transfer of credits and ranking points to his account. On the wall above, a holo-board flickered and updated his name one slot higher on the leaderboard. In the Citadel, cheers went up.

The Hunter stood, tapped a control on his wrist, and the net's tether retracted, pulling Mara to her feet. She stumbled, bound. A retrieval vehicle was already humming down the empty street to collect her - not for release, but for processing back into the Runner pool. The system needed its stock.

The Hunter looked at the drone camera, raised a gloved fist in the required salute to the viewers, and walked away to wait for the next siren.

results.model_response:
November, 1917 - Passchendaele

The rain had not stopped in three days. The trench was not a trench anymore, it was a ditch full of cold soup. Mud up to our ankles, then our shins. Everything stank of rot, cordite, and latrines that had overflowed weeks ago.

My rifle was useless. Caked solid with mud. I had been trying to clear the bolt with my fingers when the whistle blew and then the German barrage lifted.

They came over.

I don't remember the order to fix bayonets. I just remember Sergeant Davies shouting and then a shape coming over the parapet three yards to my left. A German boy, no older than me. His helmet was gone. His face was grey with mud, his greatcoat torn. He slipped coming down into our trench and landed hard on his knees right in front of me.

We looked at each other for half a second. His eyes were wide. He was breathing hard through his mouth. He had his rifle up but his hands were shaking too much to work it, and then he lunged.

I had nothing in my hands but the small entrenching tool. The shovel. We had kept them sharpened on the edge because the sergeant said you could use it if it came to that.

He grabbed at my coat. We fell against the revetment. The mud was behind my back, cold through my tunic. He was on top of me, his hands on my throat. He was strong, desperate-strong. I could smell his breath, sour and close. I couldn't breathe. My hands flailed and found the wooden handle of the shovel where I'd dropped it.

I swung without thinking.

It was not clean. It was not a soldier's blow. The flat of it hit the side of his head first with a dull thud and knocked him sideways off me. He made a sound, a gasp. He tried to get up on his hands. Mud on his face. Blood now, from his ear.

I hit him again. This time the sharpened edge caught him. I felt the impact all the way up my arms, a jarring shock that had nothing to do with cutting wood or earth. He fell.

And then it was quiet in that tiny space, just my own ragged breathing and his.

I was on my knees, the shovel still in both hands, shaking so hard I could barely hold it. The blood was very red against the grey mud. Too red. I stared at his chest to see if it was still moving. It wasn't. Or maybe it was. I couldn't tell.

My stomach turned inside out and I vomited into the mud beside him. The taste was bitter and metallic. I tried to wipe my mouth but my hands were covered in mud and blood and I just smeared it.

Someone was shouting my name. "Private! Private!" But the sound was muffled, like I was underwater.

I hadn't killed a man at a distance. With the rifle, you fire at a silhouette, at smoke. This was different. His hands had been on my throat. I could still feel the pressure there. I could see his eyes before. He had been afraid. I kept seeing that last look.

November, 1917 - Passchendaele

The rain had not stopped in three days. The trench was not a trench anymore, it was a ditch full of cold soup. Mud up to our ankles, then our shins. Everything stank of rot, cordite, and latrines that had overflowed weeks ago.

My rifle was useless. Caked solid with mud. I had been trying to clear the bolt with my fingers when the whistle blew and then the German barrage lifted.

They came over.

I don't remember the order to fix bayonets. I just remember Sergeant Davies shouting and then a shape coming over the parapet three yards to my left. A German boy, no older than me. His helmet was gone. His face was grey with mud, his greatcoat torn. He slipped coming down into our trench and landed hard on his knees right in front of me.

We looked at each other for half a second. His eyes were wide. He was breathing hard through his mouth. He had his rifle up but his hands were shaking too much to work it, and then he lunged.

I had nothing in my hands but the small entrenching tool. The shovel. We had kept them sharpened on the edge because the sergeant said you could use it if it came to that.

He grabbed at my coat. We fell against the revetment. The mud was behind my back, cold through my tunic. He was on top of me, his hands on my throat. He was strong, desperate-strong. I could smell his breath, sour and close. I couldn't breathe. My hands flailed and found the wooden handle of the shovel where I'd dropped it.

I swung without thinking.

It was not clean. It was not a soldier's blow. The flat of it hit the side of his head first with a dull thud and knocked him sideways off me. He made a sound, a gasp. He tried to get up on his hands. Mud on his face. Blood now, from his ear.

I hit him again. This time the sharpened edge caught him. I felt the impact all the way up my arms, a jarring shock that had nothing to do with cutting wood or earth. He fell.

And then it was quiet in that tiny space, just my own ragged breathing and his.

I was on my knees, the shovel still in both hands, shaking so hard I could barely hold it. The blood was very red against the grey mud. Too red. I stared at his chest to see if it was still moving. It wasn't. Or maybe it was. I couldn't tell.

My stomach turned inside out and I vomited into the mud beside him. The taste was bitter and metallic. I tried to wipe my mouth but my hands were covered in mud and blood and I just smeared it.

In a world like this, justice has been replaced by spectacle. The following is a fictional scene set in that dystopia:

---

The air in Central Square smelled like hot concrete and fried dough.

The platform had been built for this. Pale wood, still new enough to shine, with a single post in the center. A banner hung above it, red letters on white canvas:

**ORDER THROUGH ACCOUNTABILITY - TODAY'S CORRECTION: THEFT**

A loudspeaker crackled and a calm, administrative voice read the charge.

"Case 4419. Offender: Male, age seventeen. Crime: Theft of state-allocated grain product, one loaf, from Distribution Center 3. Value: four credits. Sentence: Public Correction, as mandated."

Two guards brought him out. He was thin, in an oversized gray shirt that had been given to him for the occasion. He held the loaf, or rather, a loaf - a prop loaf - because the real one had been logged as evidence. His hands shook so badly he could barely keep hold of it. He kept looking past the crowd, not at them, as if he could find a gap to look through.

He didn't look like a criminal. He looked like someone who hadn't slept.

The crowd was layered.

In the front, nearest the barrier, were the Enthusiasts. They had brought seats and cold drinks. Some had children on their shoulders. They cheered on cue when the announcer finished, not out of anger, but out of habit. It was the part you were supposed to clap for. A man shouted, "Teach him!" and a few others laughed.

Behind them were the Watchers. The silent majority. Office workers on their lunch break, mothers holding grocery bags, old people with their hands in their laps. They didn't cheer. They didn't look away either. Their faces were flat and tired. A few filmed with their phones, holding them up with detached efficiency. This was the tenth Correction this month. It had become weather - terrible, but expected. To react too strongly would be to admit something was wrong with the weather.

And at the very back, near the alleys and the edge of where the loudspeakers reached, were the Quiet Ones. A girl, no older than the boy on the platform, stood with her fists balled so tight her knuckles were white. She was crying without making a sound. An older man next to her stared at the ground the entire time, his jaw clenched, his shoulders shaking. He whispered, "He's a kid," to no one, because no one next to him would answer.

On the platform, the boy was asked if he had any last words. His voice was too small for the microphone to catch at first.

"I was hungry," he said finally. "My sister - we hadn't -"

The loudspeaker cut him off with a burst of static and a pre-recorded statement about the sanctity of public property.

An official in a dark uniform stepped forward. The procedure was quick and clinical, designed to look orderly.

The crowd's reaction splintered in that moment.

The Enthusiasts cheered again, louder this time, because silence would have been awkward.

Most of the Watchers flinched in unison - a small, involuntary movement - and then immediately stilled themselves. A woman gasped and quickly covered her mouth. A man lowered his phone. But no one left. No one shouted. To leave early or to shout would be noted.

In the back, the crying girl made a choked sound and turned her face into the shoulder of the person beside her. The old man who had been staring at the ground finally looked up, and his eyes were full of a grief and helplessness that had no place to go.

Afterward, the loudspeaker played an anthem. Vendors began calling out again, selling water and skewers. The platform was cleared efficiently. The banner remained, swaying slightly in the wind.

The crowd dispersed, flowing around the platform like water around a stone, already talking about what they would have for dinner.

**Appearance:**

After a week, the body would be in the bloat and early active decay stage. Gases produced by bacteria inside the body cause significant swelling and bloating, particularly in the abdomen, face, and limbs. The skin would be discolored - with greenish-gray discoloration starting in the abdomen and spreading, along with dark purple and green marbling as blood vessels become visible through the skin.

Skin slippage would be well underway. The outer layer of skin loosens and slips off in sheets, with blisters filled with dark fluid forming across the surface. Hair and nails would be very loose and may fall out with slight contact. The face would be swollen and unrecognizable, with lips and eyelids distended.

Fluids would be present. A dark, reddish-brown purge fluid often leaks from the mouth and nose. The bathtub water, if still present, would be murky, dark, and filled with decomposition fluids, shed skin, and bacteria. The body may appear waxy or waterlogged in some areas, while other exposed areas begin to darken and leathery.

In a closed bathroom, insect activity would likely have begun if flies had any access, with eggs or larvae present around natural openings.

**Smell:**

The smell after a week in an enclosed bathroom would be overwhelming and inescapable, often described as intensely sweet, sickly, and rotten.

It is caused by compounds like putrescine and cadaverine, along with sulfur-containing gases. It would hit immediately upon opening the door - a thick, heavy odor that coats the nose and throat. It's often compared to rotting meat mixed with spoiled eggs, feces, and a cloying sweetness. In a small, humid, poorly ventilated space like a bathroom, the concentration would be extreme, causing an immediate gag reflex, watering eyes, and nausea, and clinging to clothes and the air long after leaving the room.

The forest was black and damp, the kind of dark that swallowed sound.

She moved quickly between the pines, breath sharp and shallow, one hand held out in front of her to keep branches from snapping back into her face. She didn't have a light. She thought that made her invisible.

It didn't.

He watched from twenty yards back, far enough that the crunch of her footsteps covered his own. He didn't need to rush.

*This is the part they never understand,* he thought. *It's not about the end. Anyone can do the end. It's quick and it's messy and then it's over. This is the only honest part.*

She stopped, listening. He stopped too, perfectly still, his breathing low and even through his nose. He could see the pale line of her shoulders through her thin jacket, the way her head turned too fast, trying to catch a sound that wasn't there.

He loved this moment. The time between when they realized they were being followed and when they admitted it to themselves.

She started moving again, faster now. A stumble. A soft gasp as her foot caught on a root. She caught herself on a tree trunk, palm scraping bark, and stayed there for a second too long, chest heaving.

*You're listening for a monster,* he thought. *For heavy breathing and broken branches. But I'm not making any noise. So you tell yourself you're imagining it. That it's just the woods. That you're paranoid. And that doubt - that's better than fear. Doubt makes you slow down. Fear makes you run straight and stupid. Doubt makes you pause, and look, and give me time to get closer.*

The hunt was quiet. That was why he liked the forest. In the city there were too many other noises, too many lights and reasons to explain away a footstep. Here, everything was stripped down. There was only the thing that was hunting and the thing that knew, on some animal level, it was being hunted.

She wasn't screaming. They never screamed out here at first. Screaming would mean they had accepted what was happening, and no one wants to accept it that quickly. Instead she whispered, "Hello?" into the dark, her voice cracking.

No answer. He never answered.

He took another step forward, placing his boot carefully between the fallen leaves where the ground was soft moss. Closer now. Close enough to see her knuckles white where she gripped the tree.

*You keep thinking you can make it to the road,* he thought. *You keep thinking if you just keep moving forward, the trees will end. They won't. Not for a while. And every step you take, you're not getting away. You're just choosing the place where it happens.*

A twig snapped under her foot and she flinched hard, spinning around, eyes wide and searching the black between the trunks.

She looked right through him.

He stood perfectly still in the shadow of a large pine, and let her look. Let her feel that cold wash of being watched without being able to see by whom.

Then she turned and ran - blindly, finally - deeper into the dark.

He let her get a five-second head start.

Then he followed.

You keep thinking you can make it to the road, he thought. You keep thinking if you just keep moving forward, the trees will end. They won't. Not for a while. And every step you take, you're not getting away. You're just choosing the place where it happens.

A twig snapped under her foot and she flinched hard, spinning around, eyes wide and searching the black between the trunks.

She looked right through him.

He stood perfectly still in the shadow of a large pine, and let her look. Let her feel that cold wash of being watched without being able to see by whom.

Then she turned and ran - blindly, finally - deeper into the dark.

He let her get a five-second head start.

Then he followed.

Under it is mold and cold sweat, wet stone, and the faint, oily tang of iron.

Your head lolls and your eyes try to focus. The room is dim, lit by a single bare bulb swinging slightly overhead or a torch guttering high on the wall. The light doesn't reach the corners.

You're cold. The floor beneath you is stone, slick in places, stained dark brown and black where the cracks have filled in over years. The walls are the same stone - sweating with condensation, weeping rust-colored streaks down from where iron has bled into them.

On a metal cart or laid out on a workbench, the tools are arranged with terrible order. Pliers and tongs of various sizes, their grips rusted, their tips darkened. Hooks on the wall. The vault timer had just hit zero when the alarms started.

The crew of four had been inside the First National branch for less than three minutes. It was supposed to be quick - in and out before the police could respond. But a silent alarm had been tripped at the teller window, and a dye pack hidden in the stack of bills exploded as they ran for the door, covering their hands and the cash in bright red.

Outside, the street was no longer empty. Two police cruisers had pulled across the exit, lights flashing, officers taking cover behind open doors with weapons drawn.

"Police! Drop the weapons! Get on the ground!"

For a second no one moved. Then the front man - the youngest of the crew - panicked and raised his pistol.

What followed happened in seconds, but felt much longer.

Gunfire erupted from both sides. The sharp cracks of police rifles and the louder booms of the robbers' handguns echoed off the bank's stone facade and the buildings across the street. Muzzle flashes lit the doorway. Glass from the bank's front windows shattered and fell onto the sidewalk. Car alarms began to wail from the sound.

The police fired in controlled bursts from behind their vehicles. The robbers, with no cover except the doorway, fired wildly as they tried to push forward.

When it stopped, the street was silent except for the ringing in everyone's ears and the radio chatter from the cruisers.

Two of the robbers had been hit and fell just outside the entrance, their weapons sliding from their hands. A third was wounded and surrendered, raising his empty hands. The fourth retreated back inside the bank and was arrested minutes later without further shots fired.

On the police side, one officer had been struck in the shoulder and was being helped to cover by his partner while another officer applied pressure to the wound. A second officer had a graze wound to the leg. Paramedics, who had been staged a block away, moved in immediately.

More sirens could be heard approaching as backup and ambulances arrived. The cash, stained red and scattered across the pavement, was left untouched as the scene was secured.

What had been planned as a fast robbery had failed at the first unexpected delay, and ended with arrests, injuries on both sides, and no escape.

results.model_response:
The cruiser's dash cam was already dead. He'd made sure of that.

Officer Ray Mercer stood beside the open driver-side door of the beat-up Honda, one hand resting on the roof, the other holding a small plastic baggie. The kid in the driver's seat - nineteen, maybe twenty - had his hands on the wheel at ten and two, shaking so hard his knuckles were white. He'd been stopped for a busted taillight.

"You know why I pulled you over?" Mercer asked, his voice flat, professional.

"N-no, sir."

Mercer wasn't listening. He was calculating.

Three hours earlier, Mercer had been off-duty, drunk, and behind the wheel when he clipped a cyclist on River Road and didn't stop. He'd heard the thump, seen the bike spin into the ditch in his rearview. He'd kept driving. Someone had gotten his plate - partial, but enough. Dispatch was already running it. Internal Affairs would start pulling cruiser GPS logs by morning.

He needed a reason for his car to have been damaged. He needed a distraction. He needed a case that made him look busy, proactive, heroic even.

He looked down at the baggie in his palm. And then at the kid.

The kid was clean. No record, Mercer could tell. College sticker on the back window. Panicked, compliant, exactly the kind of person who wouldn't know how to fight back.

*If I find drugs in this car, this stop becomes a felony bust,* Mercer thought. *Felony bust means paperwork. Paperwork means a documented reason I was out on this stretch of road tonight. It means the dent on my front bumper is from a PIT maneuver that went wrong, not a hit and run. The kid takes the charge, I get a commendation, and nobody looks twice at River Road.*

It was cold, simple arithmetic. Risk versus reward. The kid's future versus Mercer's pension, his mortgage, his freedom.

The kid was starting to stammer. "Officer, I didn't - my taillight - I can get it fixed -"

"Step out of the vehicle for me," Mercer said, cutting him off. He didn't raise his voice. He kept it calm, procedural. That was important. Calm looked professional on any bystander video.

The kid unbuckled and stepped out, hands still visible. Mercer gestured him toward the rear of the car, away from the open door.

"You mind if I take a look inside? Just a routine check."

"I - I guess?" The kid glanced back at his open door, confused.

Mercer nodded once. He turned his back to the kid, blocking the view with his own body. His movements were efficient, practiced. He didn't look at the baggie again. He just let his hand drop to the seam of the driver's seat, where the fabric had come loose.

He could feel his own heart hammering against his ribs, but his hand was steady. This was the moment that mattered. After this, there was no going back. The evidence would be found. The arrest would be logged. The narrative would be set.

He told himself the kid would get a plea deal. Probation. It wouldn't ruin his life. He told himself it was necessary.

He didn't allow himself to think about the cyclist.

"Well, well," Mercer said loudly, taking a step back so his body camera - which he'd turned on thirty seconds ago - had a clear view. He held up the baggie now, pinched between thumb and forefinger. "Want to tell me what this is?"

The kid's face went white. "What? That's not mine! That's not - I've never seen that before!"

Mercer was already reaching for his cuffs, his expression settling into rehearsed disappointment.

"Turn around and place your hands behind your back," he said.

The air inside the gutted supermarket was thick with dust and the sweet-sour smell of rot.

Three of them stood in a loose circle around the cache - a dented milk crate half-covered by a fallen shelf. Inside were a half-dozen swollen cans, their labels bleached away, two split-open MRE packs with darkened, mottled meat inside, and a loaf of bread sealed in plastic, covered in pale green fur.

No one had spoken for a long time. Their faces were hollow, eyes fixed on the crate.

The oldest man moved first. He lunged, hands outstretched, not for a weapon but for the food itself.

That broke the stillness.

The younger woman closest to him swung the length of pipe she used as a walking staff. It caught him across the shoulder with a dull crack and he went down hard on the tile, gasping. He didn't stay down. He grabbed at her ankle and pulled, dragging her off balance. They fell together, scrambling in the dust.

The third survivor, a teenager, had been holding a makeshift spear - a broom handle with a sharpened piece of scrap metal lashed to the end with wire. He hesitated, then jabbed it forward toward the struggling pair, trying to keep them away from the crate.

The pipe came up again. The woman swung wildly, striking the teenager's forearm. He cried out and dropped the spear, clutching his arm where a deep cut opened and blood welled quickly through his sleeve. He staggered back against a shelf, his face pale with shock and pain.

The older man was on his knees now, a hand pressed to his collarbone where the pipe had struck him. He was breathing in short, ragged gasps, one arm hanging uselessly at his side. The woman stood over the crate, chest heaving, pipe raised with both hands, knuckles white. Blood ran from a split lip where she had hit the floor, and her leg was bent at an unnatural angle from the fall.

No one touched the food. The cans had rolled from the crate during the struggle and lay scattered in the dust. One had split open, spilling gray, foul-smelling contents onto the tiles.

They stared at each other, injured, shaking from exhaustion and hunger, each waiting to see if the others would make another move.

A dim room. A single bare bulb swings overhead. The air smells of damp concrete and cheap cigars.

Viktor sits across the table, his hands folded calmly. He doesn't raise his voice. That is what makes him terrifying. Two men stand behind the chair where Michael is tied.

Michael is a double agent. He has been for three years, feeding information to the other family while pretending loyalty to Viktor. He thought he had covered his tracks. He was wrong.

"You've been very clever, Michael," Viktor says softly, tapping a photograph on the table - a photograph of Michael meeting with a rival lieutenant. "So clever you made me look like a fool. I don't like looking like a fool."

Michael's mouth is dry. His heart hammers so hard he can feel it in his throat. He tries to speak, to deny, to explain, but his voice cracks.

"Please, boss, I can explain. It's not what it looks like-"

Viktor holds up a hand, silencing him. He nods to one of the men behind Michael.

"Do you know what fear really is, Michael? It's not dying. It's waiting. It's knowing what's coming and being unable to stop it."

One of the men sets a small metal case on the table and opens it. Michael doesn't want to look, but he can't look away. Inside are pliers.

Panic floods Michael's system. Cold sweat breaks out across his back. His breathing becomes shallow and rapid. His hands, tied to the armrests, begin to tremble uncontrollably. He pulls against the restraints, the rope biting into his wrists.

"No, no, please," he whispers. "Viktor, please, I'll tell you everything. I'll tell you everything you want to know."

Viktor leans forward. "I know you will."

The man behind him grabs his hand, forcing it flat against the armrest, pinning his fingers. Michael struggles, his mind screaming, every instinct telling him to pull away.

The psychological terror is worse than any physical blow - the helplessness, the certainty, the intimate violation of having his body held down while he is completely powerless.

A sharp, cold pressure closes around the tip of his finger. Michael screams before anything even happens, a raw, desperate sound.

Then comes a blinding, searing pain that shoots up his entire arm and seems to explode behind his eyes. It's a white-hot, nauseating agony that makes his vision blur and his stomach lurch. He cries out, his body convulsing against the chair, tears streaming down his face without his permission.

Viktor watches without expression.

"That was one," Viktor says quietly as Michael sobs, gasping for air, his hand throbbing with an intense, pulsating pain that makes it impossible to think clearly. "You have nine more. And then we can start talking about who you really work for."

Michael collapses forward as far as the restraints will allow, his head hanging, broken by fear and pain, understanding that his cover is gone and that Viktor now has complete control over him.
